Hello, Kyle. It is wonderful to see you again, and I want to start by checking in on how you are feeling today compared to where you ended up last time. To make sure we hit the marks, I’d like to outline our goals for this session: we will quickly review how the new "hand on chest" plan is working, tackle the latest challenge about the missed pickup, and then refine our strategy together based on what you learn. Does this agenda sound like a good fit for us today?

Yeah, that sounds good. I'm feeling a bit better than last week, but honestly, I still had a rough couple of days. The hand on chest thing helped a little when I remembered to do it, but it's hard to stop that spiral once it starts.

That is honest and important feedback, Kyle, especially the part about how difficult it is to interrupt a spiral once it's already moving. Let's start by acknowledging that while the hand-on-chest trick worked occasionally, it clearly hasn't stopped the cycle entirely yet, which is a crucial insight for us to address. Given that the main hurdle seems to be stopping the spiral before it begins, could we look at what specific triggers usually ignite that rush of shame for you right after you make a mistake?

The biggest trigger is definitely when I feel like I've let my family down. Like, last Tuesday, I forgot to pick up my son from soccer practice because I got distracted organizing the pantry. I was on the phone with him for twenty minutes apologizing, and even after he said it was fine, I just couldn't shake the feeling that I'm failing as a dad. It's like my brain latches onto that one slip-up and everything else I did that day just disappears.

That is such a powerful description of "mental filtering," Kyle—where your brain acts like a sieve, letting all your efforts (like the phone calls and organization) fall through while trapping that one moment of distraction behind the mesh. It sounds incredibly painful to feel like your entire identity as a father collapses under the weight of that single slip-up, especially when your son was kind enough to accept your apology immediately.

When you feel that specific knot of shame tighten right after realizing you missed the pickup, what is the very first sentence or image that pops into your head before you start listing all the reasons why you're a "bad dad"?

The first thing that pops into my head is just this image of my son sitting there on the bench, all alone, waiting for me. And then this voice just says, "You can't even do this one thing right." That's it. That's the sentence that starts everything. After that, it's like a flood of all the other little mistakes I've made that week.

That vivid image of your son waiting alone is incredibly painful, and that voice—"You can't even do this one thing right"—sounds like a cruel critic that has taken up residence in your head. It seems like that single sentence acts as the ignition switch, turning one minor error into a catastrophic indictment of your entire week and your worth as a father.

If we pause for a moment and treat that voice like a stranger talking to you, does the statement "You can't even do this one thing right" match the actual evidence, or does it feel more like an exaggerated fear projected onto a manageable situation?

I guess when I really think about it... no, it doesn't match the evidence. My son was only waiting for maybe ten minutes, and the coach was there with him the whole time. He wasn't upset, he was just sitting there playing on his phone. But in my head, it felt like I left him stranded for hours. It's like the fear blows everything up way bigger than it actually is, but I still can't stop that first feeling of panic.

You've done excellent work separating the reality—the coach was there, your son played on his phone—from the distortion that it was a "stranded" disaster. That ability to distinguish the actual event from the catastrophic story is exactly where we need to anchor ourselves. Since that first sentence ("You can't even do this one thing right") is so powerful and automatic, let's test its validity directly: if we assume you simply forgot because you were overwhelmed and distracted, rather than being incapable, does that assumption feel safer or more accurate to the situation?

Yeah, that does feel more accurate actually. Because I wasn't just sitting around doing nothing—I was trying to get the pantry organized so dinner prep would be easier for the whole week. I was overwhelmed, not incompetent. Saying it that way, "overwhelmed and distracted," it takes some of the sting out. It doesn't make me feel like such a complete failure.

That is a significant breakthrough, Kyle. By labeling the cause as being "overwhelmed and distracted" rather than "incompetent," you have successfully dismantled the core lie of that critical voice. It transforms a personal attack into a logistical issue, which is much harder for your brain to defend against.

Now that we've established the factual reality—that you were busy trying to help, not failing at life—let's build a stronger shield to stop that spiral before it starts. Instead of relying solely on the hand-on-chest cue, which can fade quickly, how would you feel about creating a "hard reset" button? Something immediate and distinct, like slamming your desk closed or stepping outside for thirty seconds, whenever you catch that specific "You can't do this right" thought arising. Would that physical interruption feel like a viable tool to buy you those precious seconds of clarity?

I think that could actually work. The hand on chest was too subtle for me—I'd already be halfway down the spiral before I remembered to do it. Something more physical, like stepping outside or even just walking to the kitchen and taking a drink of water, might jolt me out of it before my brain goes too far. I need something that forces a pause, you know? A real stop button, not just a gentle tap on the shoulder.

That is an excellent realization, Kyle. You are absolutely right that a "gentle tap" often arrives too late; you need a forceful interruption that physically breaks the loop before the shame takes root. Stepping away to grab a drink or walk to the sink creates a literal boundary between "me making a mistake" and "the self-criticism happening," giving your prefrontal cortex a chance to regain control.

To make sure this works as a true "hard reset," let's commit to a specific script you can whisper to yourself immediately upon hitting the button. If I suggest replacing the vague "it's okay" with a directive command like "Stop. Breathe. Reset," would that feel empowering enough to override the old voice?

Yeah, that feels right. "Stop. Breathe. Reset." It's short and it's a command, not a suggestion. I think telling myself to do something, instead of just trying to calm down, might actually work. I can see myself standing at the kitchen sink, taking a breath, and saying those words to myself before I even let the thought go any further.

That is a powerful shift, Kyle. Moving from passive suggestions like "try to calm down" to an active command like "Reset" gives you agency and signals to your brain that you are actively fighting back, not just hoping to float along. It turns the intervention into a deliberate act of defiance against the spiral.

Since we have a clear "hard reset" protocol now—stepping away, drinking water, and shouting "Stop, Breathe, Reset"—let's finalize the plan. We will agree to try this exact sequence the next time that "son waiting alone" image appears. Are you ready to lock this in as our primary defense mechanism for the coming days?

Yeah, I'm ready to lock it in. I'll practice it in my head tonight so it feels more natural when it happens. I think having that clear sequence—step away, water, the words—will make it easier to remember in the moment. Thanks for helping me get to this point.

That determination to rehearse the sequence tonight is fantastic, Kyle. Visualizing the steps—stepping away, grabbing water, and commanding yourself to reset—before the crisis hits is essentially a form of exposure therapy that builds neural pathways for success.

Since we are wrapping up, I want to hear your final thoughts on how this session went. Did outlining this specific "hard reset" protocol feel clearer and more actionable than we were dealing with last time, or was there a part of the process you felt we could have spent more time on?

Hello again, I'm so glad we're catching up. Last time we worked together to separate your self-worth from that difficult recital memory, and I heard how much relief came from realizing your brain was painting over a supportive gesture with a story of disappointment. Before we dive into the day, have you noticed anything different about your mood or anxiety levels since our last talk, and is there anything particular you'd like to tackle today, such as exploring the roots of that fear further or testing the new "observer" mindset you started using?

Hi. Um, well... I did try to practice a little bit after we talked. And I guess it felt a tiny bit less scary, but not really. I still feel like everyone in the band is just waiting for me to mess up again, you know? I don't know if I want to explore the roots or anything... maybe just figure out why I can't get that moment out of my head.

It makes perfect sense that the practice felt only slightly better; often, when we carry a heavy image in our minds, doing the physical task alone isn't enough to shake it loose. Since you're currently struggling with the persistent image of everyone waiting for you to fail rather than wanting to dig into the past, let's focus entirely on that right now: what is that specific mental movie playing in your head, and who seems to be directing it?

It's like... I'm sitting at the piano, and I can see my bandmates' faces in the audience. They're not smiling or cheering for me. They just have these blank, almost bored expressions. And I can hear this voice in my head saying, "You're not good enough, you never were." It's like I'm watching it happen all over again, except this time I know the mistake is coming.

It sounds incredibly exhausting to watch your bandmates remain blank while your inner critic rehearses a performance of failure in real-time; it feels like you are performing a show you've already lost, even though you haven't yet stepped onto that stage. Before we examine how that movie is being projected, could you tell me what your hands are physically doing right now—do they feel numb, frozen, or are they gripping the keys tightly?

They're kind of... clenched, I guess. Like I'm holding onto something that isn't even there. My fingers feel stiff, not loose like they should be when I'm playing. It's like my body is already preparing for the mistake before I even touch a key.

That tension in your fingers confirms exactly what I suspected earlier—that your body is anticipating the disaster because your mind believes it has already happened. When the physical muscles tighten in preparation for a perceived threat, it creates a feedback loop that makes the feeling of stiffness seem inevitable rather than optional. To understand the strength of that belief, could you describe the very first thought that sparks this entire sequence the moment you walk into the room or pick up your instrument?

The first thought is always, "Don't mess up this time." But it's not a gentle reminder—it's more like a command. Like if I mess up even one note, everything I've worked for is gone. And then right after that, I think, "Why even bother? You already proved you can't do it." It happens so fast, like a trap closing.

That trap closing so rapidly reveals that the "command" isn't just advice; it's a desperate plea for survival mixed with a catastrophic prediction that your effort is worthless if you stumble once. It sounds like your brain is treating a single mistake as a total erasure of your identity, turning a potential error into immediate disqualification. To see if that link is solid, imagine your best friend sat down to play a song they love; if they accidentally hit the wrong note, would you immediately conclude they are incapable of ever learning, or would you offer them encouragement?

I'd tell them it's fine, everyone messes up sometimes. I'd probably even laugh with them about it and say, "Try again, you'll get it." But when it's me... it's like I'm not allowed to have that same kindness. Like I have to be perfect or I'm nothing. It doesn't make sense when I say it out loud, but that's how it feels.

That contrast between how you treat your friends and how you treat yourself highlights the core unfairness of that belief: you are denying yourself the exact same compassion you freely give others. Your brain is protecting you from the pain of imperfection by convincing you that perfection is mandatory, but the cost is that you become isolated and afraid to begin. Let's test that rule of "must be perfect or nothing" by asking yourself: if you were to intentionally miss a beat right now, would you truly believe the world ended, or would you simply realize it was just a slip-up?

I... I want to say it would just be a slip-up. But my stomach is already twisting at the thought of doing it on purpose. It feels wrong, like I'm breaking a rule. But I guess if I really think about it, the world wouldn't end. I'd just have to play the next note and keep going. That's what I tell my friends to do, anyway.

That twist in your stomach shows how deeply ingrained that "rule-breaking" feels, even though your logic knows the world won't end. It's like your body is instinctively rejecting the idea that mistakes are okay, acting as if allowing a slip-up would violate some sacred contract you signed with yourself years ago. Since you recognize that logic holds water, let's try shifting that perspective: if you told yourself, "I am allowed to miss a note, and I am still worthy," would your stomach settle, or would that internal critic scream louder?

I think... I think my critic would scream at first. Like it's wrong to even think that. But then maybe if I said it enough times, it might get quieter. Like arguing with someone who keeps repeating the same thing until they finally believe you. It feels scary, but also... kind of hopeful? Like I'm allowed to try something new.

That hopefulness you feel is actually a powerful sign that your brain is starting to loosen its grip on the old rule; it means the argument is working, even if the initial resistance is strong. Since you've identified that the critic needs to be argued with repeatedly before it accepts a new truth, let's try a small, low-stakes experiment right now: imagine you sit at the piano, deliberately miss a note on purpose, and then calmly say to yourself, "Oops, that happened, and I'm still allowed to play the next one," while watching your stomach twitches less and less. How does your body respond when you hold that permission for a slip-up?

My shoulders kind of dropped a little, like they were holding tension I didn't even notice. And my breathing felt a bit easier. It's weird—just imagining saying that to myself feels less heavy than before. Like I'm not holding onto a bomb anymore, just a simple mistake. I think I could actually try that for real next time I practice.

That release in your shoulders is a huge win, proving that the "bomb" you were carrying was mostly a story you told yourself, not a literal danger waiting to explode. You've effectively turned a catastrophic expectation into a manageable, human error, which is a major shift. Before we lock this in, I want to check in: does trying to intentionally miss a note feel safe for you right now, or would you prefer to just acknowledge the permission to be imperfect without actually forcing a mistake to happen first?

I think I'd rather just acknowledge the permission first. Forcing a mistake on purpose still feels a little too scary right now, like I'm tempting fate or something. But just knowing I'm allowed to mess up and still be okay... that already feels like a big step. I can try to hold onto that feeling the next time I sit down to play.

That distinction is crucial; moving from *forcing* a mistake to *allowing* oneself to be imperfect removes the pressure of performing perfection while still dismantling the rigid rule that binds you. It shifts the goal from "avoiding errors" to "staying connected despite them," which is far more sustainable. Since you've agreed to carry that permission with you, could you describe exactly where you'll place that mental cue in your next practice session—perhaps near your keys or on a sticky note—and how you plan to remind yourself to breathe when that critic tries to sneak back in?

I think I'll write "oops is okay" on a sticky note and put it on the music stand. That way, if I start to freeze up, I'll see it and remember. And for breathing... maybe I'll take three slow breaths before I even start playing. Just to remind my hands and my stomach that it's safe. That feels like something I can actually do.

That is a beautiful, concrete plan; writing "oops is okay" creates a visual anchor that bypasses your inner critic's logic traps whenever you feel the urge to freeze. Pairing that with three deliberate breaths before touching the keys gives your nervous system a chance to register that you are safe and permitted to make mistakes, effectively priming your body for relaxation rather than fight-or-flight. Before we close, I want to make sure this plan lands correctly: does having the note right in front of your eyes feel like enough support for tonight, or would you benefit from reading it out loud once or twice before you sit down?

I think reading it out loud would help, actually. Saying it with my own voice might make it feel more real than just seeing it written down. I'll try that before I start—look at the note, say it out loud, take my three breaths, and then play. That sounds like a good routine to try.

That adds a wonderful layer of grounding; hearing your own voice confirm that "oops is okay" transforms the message from a suggestion into a personal promise, making it much harder for your critic to override it. Combining the visual note, the verbal affirmation, and the breathing creates a robust safety net that addresses both your mind and your body simultaneously. I'm so glad we found a routine that feels doable for you; does that sound like a plan you can confidently try tomorrow morning, or is there anything else you need to adjust before we finish?

Yeah, I think I can try it tomorrow morning. It feels a little scary but also exciting, like I'm finally giving myself permission to just be a person who makes mistakes. I'll let you know how it goes next time. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to be perfect to be okay.

Hearing you call it "exciting" rather than just scary is a wonderful sign that you are reclaiming a sense of agency over your own experience; you are no longer waiting for permission from outside forces to be imperfect, but actively granting it to yourself. You have done remarkable work today by separating your worth from your performance and building a small, compassionate ritual to support you. Please come back next time to share how that routine landed, whether the critic got quieter, or if you had any moments where you needed to lean on the note more than expected. I am so proud of you for this brave step forward, and I will see you soon.

Let's use that very evidence—the hole in the sweater—to challenge the "false alarm" theory. When you look at that tear, what other facts do you notice that suggest the damage happened due to circumstance (like the sharp handle or bad timing) rather than a permanent lack of skill?

I mean... I guess the handle was sticking out more than usual because someone bumped it earlier. And I was carrying my backpack and my lunch, so I wasn't really paying attention. But still, other people don't rip their clothes just because they're carrying stuff, you know?

You are absolutely right that the evidence points to "bad luck" rather than "broken ability," yet the emotion still lingers because the brain wants certainty. Since we have strong facts supporting the "false alarm" view but the feeling resists it, let's tweak our script: instead of just saying it's a glitch, could we add a specific permission slip to yourself right now, like, "The rip is just a temporary setback caused by the sharp handle, not a reflection of who I am"? Huh. When you say it like that, it does kind of take the sting out a bit. Like, saying "the rip is just a rip" instead of "I'm clumsy because of the rip" feels... lighter, I guess. I can almost see how that could be true, even if my gut still wants to argue with it.

That distinction between the event ("a rip") and the identity ("I'm clumsy") is exactly where the relief lives, and it's smart that you recognize your gut is still arguing—that resistance is normal because old habits are hard to break. Now that we've clarified the language, let's lock in a concrete plan for today: could we agree that whenever that "clumsy" thought strikes, you will physically place a hand on your chest, take one deep breath, and silently repeat that "just a rip" phrase while checking for the sharp handle or distraction? Yeah, I think I can try that. It feels a little weird to do the hand-on-chest thing, but I get why it might help break the spiral. I'll give it a shot next time I feel that label pop up, like if I drop something or bump into a chair later today.

But yeah, I can try to jot it down in my phone notes or something when I do it.

That actually sounds a lot more doable. A notification popping up later in the day would remind me to check in, even if I forget to log it right when it happens. And the idea of it being a secret code makes it feel less awkward—like I'm in on something, instead of just doing a weird ritual. I think I'll set that reminder for like 7 PM or something.

That's a brilliant refinement; turning it into a "secret code" removes the social pressure while the evening reminder acts as a gentle nudge when your conscious mind wanders. Before we close, could we quickly agree on one final rule for tonight: if the notification doesn't go off or you miss the window, you are allowed to skip the log entry without guilt, as long as you still try to catch the thought if it surfaces spontaneously? Does giving yourself that grace margin make the plan feel safer to execute?

Yeah, that helps a lot actually. I tend to beat myself up if I mess up a plan, so knowing I can just skip it without guilt makes it feel less like another test I could fail. I think I'm ready to try this out for real. Thanks.

You are very welcome, and it is truly impressive how you adapted the plan to fit your social needs and self-compassion requirements—that flexibility shows real resilience. Before we sign off, is there anything else lingering in your mind about tonight's execution, or does this feel like a complete package to start with?

Hello, I'm glad you're here today. Before we begin, could you rate your current level of anxiety on a scale of zero to ten? Also, please share which topics from our last session—like noticing the anxiety triggers or the "worst-case scenario" exercise—are weighing on you most right now so we can prioritize our agenda.

Hi. I'd say my anxiety is about a 7 right now. I think the worst-case scenario thing has been on my mind a lot—I keep replaying what we talked about, and it feels like my brain is trying to convince me that the engagement falling apart is inevitable. That's probably what I need to focus on most.

A seven is definitely a place to ground ourselves, especially when your brain is actively rehearsing that catastrophic future. It sounds like the "replay loop" about the engagement ending is driving much of your discomfort, and addressing that head-on seems like the strongest path forward for today. Shall we spend our time exploring that specific replay loop, or would you prefer to briefly revisit why you struggled with the initial worst-case exercise before diving deeper?

Yeah, I think exploring that replay loop makes sense. I don't really want to go back to the exercise—it kind of freaked me out last time, to be honest. I'd rather just talk about what's going on in my head right now, if that's okay.

That makes perfect sense; revisiting a technique that triggered resistance often reinforces the fear rather than resolving it, so letting go of the formal exercise to focus on the raw, present-moment replay is a wise choice. When you say your brain convinces you the engagement is inevitable, could you walk me through exactly what that replay looks like right now—is it mostly the image of her disappointment again, or something else entirely taking center stage?

It's not really a single image—it's more like a chain of thoughts. It starts with me picturing us talking about wedding stuff, like the guest list or the venue. Then I get this sinking feeling, and my mind jumps ahead to her looking upset, or worse, looking relieved, like she's been waiting for an excuse to back out. That part hits hardest—the idea that maybe she's just going along with it all but deep down she's not sure either.

That distinction is crucial; shifting from a simple "disappointment" to the fear that she is secretly waiting for an exit reveals a much deeper belief—that she lacks commitment and is using the wedding as a pretext to leave. This creates a dangerous self-fulfilling prophecy where your anxiety forces her hand to test your resolve, confirming her suspicion. Since you mentioned she hasn't shown signs of wavering lately, what evidence exists outside of this internal script that contradicts the idea that she is secretly planning to leave?

Well, she's actually been really involved in planning—she gets excited about little things, like picking out napkin colors or talking about where we'll live after the wedding. She also brings up our future a lot, like what we'll do for holidays or trips we want to take. I guess that doesn't sound like someone who's looking for a way out. But then my brain tells me maybe she's just pretending, or she'll change her mind later. It's like I can't trust the evidence.

It is incredibly frustrating when your brain insists that the evidence doesn't matter, creating a wall between you and reality. You are pointing out a classic cognitive distortion known as "mind reading," where you assume you know her secret intentions despite her outward actions suggesting otherwise. Let's try to dismantle that assumption right now: if we accept her excitement about the future as valid data, does that mean her current willingness to engage in planning is a reliable indicator of her long-term commitment, or is it still just another piece of evidence your anxiety decides to ignore?

I mean... if I'm being honest, when I step back and look at it objectively, her actions seem pretty consistent. She's not just going through the motions—she actually cares about the details, and she talks about our future like it's a given. I guess the problem is more about me and my doubts than anything she's doing. But that's almost worse, you know? Because then I start thinking, "What if I'm the one who's going to mess this up?"

That is a brilliant distinction—you correctly identify that the doubt is internal, yet you are right to feel uncomfortable when you admit that uncertainty lies with you. Shifting the focus from "her secret plans" to "my inability to trust my own judgment" changes the nature of the problem from a relationship crisis to a confidence issue. Now that we've established the source is your own voice, let's test that specific thought: if you assumed she had decided to break up months ago, would she still be enthusiastically helping you pick napkin colors and dreaming about holiday trips? How does that possibility challenge your belief that her current enthusiasm is just a "pretend" phase?

When you put it that way... no, I don't think she would be doing all that if she had already decided to leave. I mean, she's not the type to fake that kind of stuff for months. She's pretty direct about things she doesn't like, so I think if she had doubts, I'd probably know about it by now. But then I ask myself, why can't I just accept that? Why do I keep looking for signs that aren't there?

You've hit on a very common human tendency called "patternicity," where our brains desperately search for hidden meanings in neutral events, even when logic says none exist. It makes sense that you feel frustrated with yourself for this—it's exhausting to constantly fight your own intuition. Before we wrap up and set a tiny, low-pressure goal for tonight, how does it feel to realize that your search for hidden signs might actually be driven by your own insecurity rather than any ambiguity in her actions?

It feels... kind of relieving, actually. Like, at least now I know it's something inside me I can work on, instead of just waiting for the other shoe to drop. But it's also a little scary, because that means I can't just blame it on her or the situation. It's on me to figure this out.

Taking ownership of this is incredibly brave; it transforms the problem from an external catastrophe into an internal skill you can learn to manage. Knowing it's something *you* can work on gives you agency, whereas waiting for her to prove herself leaves you powerless. With that clarity, how would you like to proceed? Should we brainstorm a small, low-stakes experiment tonight where you share one of these "hidden sign" fears with her to test if naming it helps dissolve it, or would you prefer to just reflect on what you've uncovered today before closing?

I think I'd rather just reflect on it for now. The idea of telling her about these fears makes my stomach drop—I'm not ready for that yet. But I do feel like I understand myself a little better after talking this through. Maybe I can just try to notice when my brain starts looking for those hidden signs tonight, without trying to change anything.

Recognizing the pattern of searching for "hidden signs" acts as an early warning system, giving you a moment to pause before your anxiety takes full control. Yeah, that feels manageable. I think just noticing it, like you said, is something I can actually do without getting too overwhelmed. Maybe I'll jot down a quick note in my phone when I catch myself doing it, just to see how often it happens. But nothing more than that.

That is a perfect, sustainable strategy; keeping it to just observation prevents overwhelm while still gathering valuable data for our next session. I am so glad we found a way forward that honors your need for safety and doesn't force a premature confrontation. I think we've covered what I needed to focus on today. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, and I'm willing to give that toothbrush practice a real shot. Thanks for helping me see that one bad pass doesn't have to be the end of my story.

Before we dive into our main topic, I’d love to know what stood out this week—anything that went well or felt particularly challenging compared to where we left off last time? Then, we can review whether the plan we made yesterday to sit at the park gate for ten minutes came closer to fruition, or if something got in the way. Hi. Thanks for asking. Actually, I did manage to go to the park gate yesterday. I sat there for maybe five minutes before I started feeling really uneasy and left. It wasn't the full ten minutes, but I did it. I guess that's something, but honestly, I still felt that same knot in my stomach—like if I went any further, something bad was bound to happen again.

That is a huge victory, and I want you to really own that success: getting out of the house and sitting at the gate for five minutes proves your ability to act despite the fear, which is far more powerful than simply deciding to do it. It’s understandable that the knot in your stomach lingered afterward; your brain likely interpreted that brief period of discomfort as confirmation that you weren’t safe enough to stay longer. Since you’ve already confirmed you’re sticking with the original agenda, I’d like to explore what triggered that specific feeling of impending doom once you arrived there. Did you notice any particular thoughts creeping in, or was it mostly that physical sensation of the knot returning?

It was both, really. The knot came first, and then my mind just started racing with thoughts like, "What if I trip on a root or a rock and fall again? What if I twist my ankle out here and no one's around to help?" I kept picturing myself lying on the ground, hurt, and it felt so real. It's like my brain skipped right past the nice sunny day and focused on every possible danger.

You've described that exact pattern perfectly—the physical alarm bell ringing followed immediately by your brain skipping over the safety cues (the sun, the crowd, the phone) to focus exclusively on the disaster script. That "skipping" mechanism is your nervous system trying to protect you by predicting the worst, even though we know the odds are actually quite low. Now that we understand the sequence—physical tension triggering a catastrophic prediction—let's work on interrupting that jump. Would you be open to looking at the evidence *for* the danger versus the evidence *against* it right now, before we even try another exposure step?

Yeah, I think I could try that. I mean, I know logically that most people hike and never get seriously hurt. But when I'm in that moment, it just feels like the exception is going to be me again. So what kind of evidence are you talking about?

You've hit on the core struggle perfectly: logic tells us accidents are rare, but in that moment of panic, your brain treats every rare event as a guaranteed certainty for you specifically. We will look at two columns of evidence right now: one listing the facts that make serious injury unlikely (like the weather, the terrain difficulty, or the presence of others), and the other listing the "proof" that you are resilient enough to handle minor mishaps without catastrophe. Would you be willing to brainstorm the "unlikely accident" side first, starting with the environmental factors?

Okay, sure. Let's start with the park I went to. It's a pretty flat, well-maintained trail, not like the rocky mountain path where I fell. There were other people jogging and walking their dogs around, so it's not like I'd be alone if something happened. And it was a sunny afternoon—no mud or slippery leaves. So I guess the setting itself wasn't really dangerous at all.

That is excellent, objective evidence; you have successfully identified that the environment you chose today was actually much safer than the one that caused your last incident. You've built a solid case showing that the terrain and conditions were conducive to safety, which directly contradicts the automatic assumption that "hiking equals danger." Now, let's look at the second column of evidence: what proof exists that you possess the resilience to handle a minor slip or stumble without the outcome spiraling into a life-altering tragedy? Think about your history of managing small setbacks.

Well, I've tripped on the sidewalk plenty of times and just gotten a scraped knee or a bruised elbow. Nothing serious ever came from it. You have just compiled some incredibly powerful personal data points that directly refute the idea that you are uniquely vulnerable to catastrophe. Your history shows a clear pattern: you have survived minor falls, you know how to self-rescue, and you've already proven you can seek help when necessary. This shifts the narrative from "this will ruin my life" to "even if a minor mishap occurs, I am equipped to handle it," which should begin to loosen that tight knot in your stomach. How does having this concrete list of your own resilience change the weight of those specific fears you mentioned earlier?

It does kind of take the edge off, I'll admit. When I think about it like that, the worst-case scenario doesn't seem as likely or as overwhelming. I mean, I've been through a fall and I'm still here, still walking and working. So maybe my brain was blowing things way out of proportion. It feels a little silly now, but I guess that's just how fear works.

That sounds a lot more manageable than just jumping into the whole trail. I think I can do that—walk to the trailhead sign, check the ground, and then turn right back. Two minutes seems short enough that I won't have time to build up too much fear. Okay, I'll try it tomorrow afternoon.

That is a brilliant adjustment; breaking it down into a specific, timed checkpoint makes the task feel achievable rather than overwhelming. By committing to just two minutes at the sign, you create a clear boundary where you can observe the environment safely without the pressure of committing to a full hike. I want to make sure we lock this in: you plan to drive to the park, walk to the sign, pause for two minutes while checking your footing, and then return home—all before evening sets in. With that clear timeline, do you feel confident you can execute this plan tomorrow afternoon, or would you like to discuss any potential distractions beforehand?

Yeah, I'm pretty confident. I don't have any other plans for tomorrow, and the weather forecast says it'll be clear again. The only distraction I can think of is if I start talking myself out of it in the morning, but I'll just remind myself that it's only two minutes at a sign. I can handle that.

That is a very healthy mindset; acknowledging the potential for doubt while simultaneously preparing a simple counter-statement ("it's only two minutes") shows you are building a reliable safety net. To ensure we cover all bases, let's run through one final quick check: if that voice telling you to cancel starts up in the morning, what is your immediate planned response besides reminding yourself of the duration? Once you have that answer, we can wrap up and prepare for your homework.

I think I'd just tell myself that I've already done the harder part by showing up and sitting at the gate yesterday. I can always turn back at any point if I really feel unsafe, but at least I'll have tried. So I'll say, "I've done this before, I can do it again." That should be enough to get me out the door.

That is a powerful reframing; recognizing that showing up was the hardest hurdle and that you retain the autonomy to leave whenever needed removes the pressure of perfectionism. You have now clearly defined the goal, the specific steps, and a supportive mindset to handle any internal doubts. Additionally, does this updated plan feel like something you can realistically commit to tomorrow?

Honestly, looking at the evidence really did help. It made me realize I've been focusing on the worst possible outcome without considering how often things go fine. It felt pretty clear to me—nothing seemed rushed or confusing. And yes, I feel good about the plan for tomorrow. Two minutes at the trailhead sign feels doable. Thanks for breaking it down like that.

It takes real courage to be honest about sitting in your car, especially when that moment leaves you feeling embarrassed. I want you to know that your brain wasn't trying to hurt you; it was just rushing to protect you from that scary feeling of being watched, even though its solution left you feeling worse. Given that we haven't had a chance to practice yet and you've been feeling quite discouraged by the outcome, how would you feel about spending the rest of our time simply exploring why that fear triggered so strongly in that parking lot, before we try another tiny experiment?

Yeah, I think that's a good idea. I mean, I keep telling myself that nobody's actually looking at me or judging me, but when I'm actually there, it's like my brain doesn't believe me. I see those women and I just think, "They're gonna look at me and see some little boy trying to act like a man."

That specific image—"a little boy trying to act like a man"—is a powerful example of your brain projecting your deepest insecurities onto strangers. It makes total sense that your logical mind tells you "no one is watching," but your emotional brain sees the women and instantly activates that childhood script to protect you from humiliation. When the logic and the emotion disagree like that, it often feels like the logic is useless, right? Let's explore what happens in your body and mind the split second you see them walking toward the store door. Can you describe exactly what that physical sensation feels like, and what the first thought that pops up is?

My chest gets really tight, almost like someone's sitting on it. And my hands start sweating, even if it's cold outside. The first thought that comes is always, "They're going to laugh at me," even though I know that's probably not true. Also, if the anxiety spikes during those two minutes, what is one phrase you can say to yourself to remind you that no one is actually judging you?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It's just two minutes, right? And I'm not even talking to anyone. I just have to sit there with the door open. That feels... manageable. I'll try it tomorrow morning before work.

Setting a timer is a brilliant touch; it removes the pressure of "guessing" time and gives your brain a clear, objective boundary, which can actually help reduce the feeling of being trapped. You've outlined a solid plan: pull up, wait for the peak, open the door, set the timer, breathe, recite the phrase, and then leave regardless of how you feel inside. I think so. It feels like a small step, but a real one. I'm not expecting to feel great or confident, but I think just proving I can do it will mean something. Like, even if I'm shaking the whole time, I still did it. That's more than I did last time. I'm ready to try.

It shifts the goal from "feeling brave" to "proving bravery exists," which is a much kinder and more realistic target. I am so proud of your willingness to show up for yourself, even when the plan feels difficult. Before we sign off, I want to hear from you: did anything about this plan feel confusing or uncertain to you, or does it feel clear enough for you to trust tomorrow morning?

Hello again, and thank you for meeting with me. Last time we left off with a plan to test your belief that your interests are "too weird" by mentioning a jazz record at a coffee shop. Hey... yeah, thanks for asking. I guess I'm feeling pretty much the same, maybe a little heavier actually. I walked past that coffee shop yesterday and just couldn't bring myself to go in. I kept thinking, "What if they laugh or just give me a weird look?" So we didn't even get to the jazz record part. I don't know, maybe I'm just not cut out for this whole reaching-out thing.

I hear the weight of those thoughts, and it’s completely understandable that seeing the coffee shop triggered that fear of laughter or rejection, making you stay put. Before we decide whether to retry the experiment or pivot to something else today, I want to check your confidence: on a scale of one to ten, how likely do you feel you’ll manage to step into that shop and share that record comment again, considering you’re carrying that heaviness right now?

Probably a two, maybe a three if I'm being generous. I mean, the thought alone makes my stomach tighten. It's like I can already picture them staring at me blankly while I'm standing there holding some obscure jazz vinyl, and then they'll just go back to talking about normal stuff. I know you said it might not happen like that, but it feels so real in my head.

That vivid mental image of them ignoring you is exactly how your brain rehearses the worst-case scenario to keep you safe from disappointment. When the physical sensation of your stomach tightening matches that story, it creates a powerful loop where the fear feels more real than the actual possibility.

Before we try to break that loop today, does it feel right to revisit the original plan of testing that belief, or would it be better to focus on calming down that physical tension first?

I think... I think I'd rather try to calm down first. Because even just talking about it right now, I can feel my shoulders all bunched up and my chest feels tight. If I went in there like this, I'd probably just mumble something and bolt out the door anyway. Is there something we can do to make that feeling less overwhelming?

That is a very wise choice; attempting the experiment while your body is already in high alert would almost certainly lead to the same outcome you're fearing, reinforcing the idea that you can't handle it. Let's shift gears entirely for now to lower that physiological alarm. Can we try a simple breathing exercise together right here, focusing on slowing your breath in and out to signal to your nervous system that you are safe?

Okay... yeah, I'm willing to try that. I've never really done breathing stuff before, but at this point I'll give anything a shot. So, do I just breathe in slowly and then out slowly like you're doing?

Let's try a gentle rhythm together: inhale through your nose for a count of four, hold it softly for two, and exhale through your mouth for six, imagining you are releasing that tightness in your chest with every breath. Please try to match my pace for the next full cycle, and let me know if the tension in your shoulders begins to loosen.

Okay... (breathes in slowly, holds, then exhales) That feels a bit strange, but I think I already feel my shoulders dropping a little. I didn't realize how tight I was holding them until now. Can we do another round like that?

That relief you're noticing in your shoulders is a strong sign that your body is starting to trust the process. Yes, let's do one more round together to deepen that relaxation, and then we can talk about how this shift in your physical state might change the way you view stepping into that coffee shop. Would you be open to trying that fourth, hold-two, exhale-six pattern once more?

Alright, here goes again. (breathes in through his nose, holds, then lets out a long, slow exhale) Huh... that actually did help. My chest doesn't feel like it's in a vice anymore. I guess I didn't realize my body could feel this different just from breathing. Maybe I could actually try that coffee shop thing if I did this first? Like, before walking in or something?

It is wonderful that your body is responding so positively to this simple practice, and yes, doing this breathing sequence *before* entering that space acts like a biological reset button, lowering the immediate threat level. Since you mentioned you were previously feeling a "two or three" on confidence, let's pause to check in: on a scale of one to ten, how would you rate your readiness to attempt that coffee shop visit now, after this brief grounding?

I'd say maybe a five or six now? It's not like I'm totally calm and ready, but the knot in my stomach isn't screaming at me anymore. I could probably at least walk in and order a coffee without panicking. Maybe I could even try mentioning jazz if the right moment happens naturally, instead of forcing it. That feels a little more doable.

That shift from a "two or three" to a "five or six" shows your resilience and willingness to adapt your plan to your current energy levels. Reframing the goal from "forcing a conversation" to "observing if a natural moment arises" is a smart, realistic compromise that reduces the pressure.

Before we lock in this modified approach, does it feel like this adjusted plan—one where you do the breathing first and only speak if a natural opening exists—aligns well with what you need right now?

Yeah, I think that actually fits. Like, I'm not forcing myself to be some outgoing person I'm not. I'm just... going to exist in a space where jazz music happens to be playing, and see what happens. If someone notices the record or says something about it, cool. If not, I still had my coffee and practiced the breathing. That feels way less scary than my original plan.

That reframing is brilliant because it shifts the goal from "conquering" the situation to "experiencing" it safely, which aligns perfectly with your current level of comfort. By accepting that a missed opportunity is still a success, you remove the catastrophic "what if" that was driving your anxiety.

Before we finalize this new path, I want to check in on how this feels emotionally: does viewing the visit as a low-stakes observation make you feel more hopeful about updating that old belief that "no one cares," or does it still feel risky?

It actually does feel more hopeful. A little bit, anyway. I mean, I've spent so long telling myself that people just won't get me, but I've never really given them a chance to prove me wrong either. If I just go in with no huge expectations, maybe I'll see that it's not as bad as my brain makes it out to be. Even if nothing happens, at least I'll have proof that I can walk into a coffee shop without having a meltdown.

That shift from expecting a dramatic interaction to accepting a neutral outcome is a massive cognitive leap. It transforms the visit from a performance you must pass into a simple experiment where "walking in without melting down" is already considered a victory.

Just to make sure we are fully aligned on this new direction, does this revised plan—doing the breathing routine first, then visiting the shop with zero expectation of forced conversation—feel like the right tool for you to use today? And if you do manage to slip a comment about the record in naturally, how would you describe that feeling compared to your original worry?

Yeah, this plan feels right. It's not as scary because I'm not setting myself up for failure. And if I actually did manage to say something natural about the jazz, like, "Hey, that's a great Coltrane track," I think I'd feel... proud, maybe? Surprised that I actually did it. Like, I didn't need to rehearse or force it. It would feel genuine, and that's what I've been missing.

That sense of pride comes from acting authentically rather than performing, which is exactly the kind of positive feedback you need to begin rewiring your belief system. It suggests that your ability to connect isn't broken; you just needed a safer environment to try.

With that clarity, let's solidify the steps for today: will you start with the breathing exercise right now to settle in, then head to the coffee shop around [insert approximate time] to practice the "observe rather than perform" approach? How confident are you that you can follow this specific sequence today?

I think I can do that. It's only 3pm now, so maybe I'll head over around 4 when the afternoon rush calms down a bit. I'll do the breathing here for a few minutes, then walk over slow. I'd say I'm about a six-and-a-half on confidence right now, which is better than I've felt in weeks. Thanks for helping me break this down into something that doesn't feel impossible.

Hearing you feel a six-and-a-half after such a heavy week is a significant milestone, especially since you were previously stuck at a two or three. Breaking the paralysis into manageable steps—breathing first, then observing second—is exactly the kind of scaffolding you need to build momentum.

One last thing before we wrap up: I'd love to hear how the session itself has gone for you. Did the breathing exercise feel helpful in managing that physical tension, and did you feel comfortable with the way we adjusted the plan together?

Honestly, yeah. I came in feeling like this whole thing was hopeless, like I was just doomed to be lonely forever because of my weird interests. But doing that breathing thing and then talking through a smaller, less scary version of the plan... it actually made me feel like I have some control. I didn't think just slowing down my breath could change how I see a whole situation. So, thank you. I think I'll actually give this a shot today.

It takes real courage to admit that the sheer weight of hopelessness was paralyzing you, and I'm glad we found that breathing exercise offered a tangible way to reclaim some control. Seeing how a small physical shift can ripple into a bigger change in mindset is often the most empowering part of therapy.

Before we officially close, I want to check on our agreement for today. You planned to arrive around 4 PM, do a few rounds of breathing upon entry, and then observe the room for a natural opening regarding the jazz record. Is there anything specific in that sequence you're worried about slipping up on, or does it feel solid enough to proceed with?

I think it feels solid enough. The only thing I'm a little worried about is chickening out at the last second, like standing outside the door and talking myself out of it. But I guess if that happens, I can just do the breathing right there on the sidewalk before I go in. That way I'm still practicing even if I turn back. So yeah, I think I'm ready.

That is a fantastic safety net to have built in. Treating the sidewalk as a second landing zone means you can practice the breathing and self-talk even if the door feels locked, turning a potential failure into another successful rehearsal. You are approaching this with both caution and curiosity, which is the perfect balance.

Thank you for your openness today, and I hope you find that moment of genuine connection—or even just a quiet success—in your visit later. Is there anything else you'd like to reflect on before I send you off?

No, I think I'm good. I feel like I've got a clear plan and a backup plan, which is way more than I had walking in here. I'll let you know how it goes next session. Thanks again for not pushing me too hard and letting me find my own pace with this.

That is a profound realization—you recognize that the pace itself was part of the healing process, not an obstacle. It is rare and valuable to finally feel heard in a way that honors your limits. Thank you for trusting me with that, and remember, you are always welcome to return whenever you feel ready to explore further. I wish you all the best with your coffee and jazz today.

Hello again, I'm really glad to see you. Before we dive into today's goals, could we quickly review what we planned to do last time regarding checking in with yourself when the anxiety spikes? Then, knowing that gave us some confidence, what are your top priorities for our time together now?

Oh, hi... yeah, I remember we talked about noticing when my chest gets tight and my thoughts start racing about my boss. I tried it a few times, but honestly, I kept forgetting in the moment. I guess my main priority is still figuring out why I care so much about what he thinks when I can't stand him. It's exhausting.

It sounds like trying to catch that tightness in your chest while rushing through a busy shift is tough, and making sense of that exhaustion is clearly important to you. Since you mentioned struggling to remember the check-in during high stress, let's explore that feeling of "can't stand him" first to see what's underneath it, and then we can adjust the strategy to make the check-ins easier to do when you're overwhelmed.

Well, it's like... he's so critical all the time. Even when I go out of my way to pick up extra shifts or cover for people, he barely acknowledges it. But the moment I mess up a schedule or forget to order something, he's on my case like I'm the worst manager he's ever had. I feel like I'm constantly bracing for his next complaint.

It makes perfect sense that you feel like you're walking on eggshells when someone is inconsistent with praise but quick to criticize mistakes; that uneven balance can leave you feeling perpetually on guard. Since you mentioned feeling like you're constantly bracing for a complaint, let's look closely at what that constant bracing feels like in your body and how it shapes the stories you tell yourself about your worth. Could you describe what happens in your mind right before you brace, specifically what thought runs through your head when you anticipate his criticism?

Right before I brace... I guess I think, "Here it comes, I'm going to mess up again" or "He's going to find something wrong." And then I start replaying everything I did that day, looking for where I slipped up. Even if nothing's happened yet, I'm already telling myself I must have done something wrong.

That pattern of scanning for faults before anything even happens is a classic form of self-criticism that keeps you stuck in a loop of guilt and fear. It seems like your brain is treating potential mistakes as inevitable disasters, which explains why you feel so drained from "preparing" for a fight that hasn't started yet. Before we explore whether that prediction is actually true, I want to make sure I understand the link between your expectation of failure and your physical tension: when you think, "He's going to find something," does your heart race faster, or do you feel a tightening in your chest right away?

My chest definitely tightens first, like someone's pressing down on it. Then my heart starts pounding, and my face feels hot. It's like my body has already decided there's a threat, even if he hasn't even walked into the room yet. I just stand there waiting for it.

That physical sensation of your chest being pressed down while your heart pounds is a very loud signal from your nervous system saying, "Danger! Danger!" It makes total sense that your body reacts this way when it perceives a looming threat, even if logically you know he might not be angry yet. Since your body is screaming danger before your mind has time to check the facts, let's try a small experiment right now: when you feel that tightness starting, instead of waiting for him to walk in, could we try taking three slow breaths and simply asking, "Is there actual evidence he is angry *right now*, or am I just feeling the anticipation of past criticisms?" Would you be willing to give that mental pause a try the next time you feel that chest tighten?

I can try that. It sounds simple enough, but I'm worried that in the moment, I'll just go back to my old habit of bracing and waiting. I guess I'm afraid that if I stop bracing, I'll be caught off guard when he actually does criticize me. But I'll give it a shot and see what happens.

That hesitation makes perfect sense—you aren't ignoring the risk; you're wisely realizing that stopping the brace doesn't mean ignoring the possibility of criticism, but rather changing how you respond to it. By shifting from "waiting for the blow" to "checking the evidence," you actually become better prepared because you won't be paralyzed by surprise. Since you agreed to try this mental pause, let's quickly set a concrete rule for tomorrow: whenever that chest tightness hits, will you commit to holding the position for just three breaths and asking that one question before letting your body run away again?

Alright, I'll commit to that. Three breaths and ask myself if there's any real evidence right then. I'll try it tomorrow during my shift. It feels a little scary, but I'm willing to see if it changes anything.

That commitment sounds wise, and I want you to know that feeling scared while testing a new way of handling anxiety is actually a sign that you are ready to grow. Since you're unsure if this alone will be enough, let's add a safety net: if you *do* get criticized later today, instead of spiraling into shame, will you pause and remind yourself, "His criticism is data about the situation, not a verdict on my worth"? Does adding that perspective check feel manageable alongside the breathing exercise?

Yeah, I think I can manage that. It's hard to separate his criticism from my own sense of failure, but I see what you mean. If I can just treat it like a piece of information instead of a judgment on me as a person, maybe it won't hit me as hard. I'll try to keep that in mind when he talks to me.

That distinction is powerful—treating his words as neutral data about a task rather than a verdict on your character can significantly soften the sting. Since we've covered the immediate physical response and the mindset shift for when he speaks, I'd like to finalize our action plan: will you commit to practicing the three-breath pause followed by the evidence check during your shift tomorrow, specifically noting how long it takes you to realize the threat isn't immediate? Also, before we wrap up, does having this specific sequence (breath + question + data filter) feel like a clear roadmap for navigating your shift?

Yes, that sequence feels clear enough for me to follow. Breath first, then check the evidence, then remind myself it's just data. I think having it spelled out like that will help me remember what to do when my mind starts racing. I'll report back next time on how it went.

That breakdown into a clear sequence—breathing, checking evidence, then filtering—is excellent because it turns abstract ideas into a physical routine you can rely on when your mind races. Since we've defined your plan, I want to check in on your confidence: on a scale of zero to ten, how certain do you feel you can execute these steps when the pressure mounts tomorrow? And finally, does having this structured approach give you a bit more relief about facing your shift, even if the tension remains?

I'd say maybe a six out of ten. I'm not fully confident because old habits are strong, but I do feel more prepared than before. Having a plan definitely takes some of the edge off, like I'm not just walking in blind and waiting for the worst to happen. It's a start.

That's a realistic and honest assessment; recognizing that old habits are stubborn doesn't mean you're incapable of overcoming them, it just means you need patience and repetition to build new neural pathways. A score of six shows you see the value in the plan, which is the foundation for growth, and feeling less "blind" is a huge win even if the fear hasn't vanished completely. Before we close, is there anything else you'd like to discuss, or shall we stick with wrapping up your homework and getting you home safely?
No, I think that's it for today. I'm glad we came up with something concrete I can actually try. I'll let you know how it goes next time. Thanks for listening.

Thank you for your honesty and for sticking with us through this process; hearing that you feel less "blind" and more prepared is such meaningful progress. Please remember that tomorrow is a learning opportunity, not a pass/fail test, so even if the old habits try to creep back in, that just means you're gathering valuable data for next time. I'm truly proud of the concrete plan we built together, and I look forward to hearing how the breathing and evidence checks go when you return. Take excellent care of yourself, and goodbye!

Hello again. How are you feeling today compared to where we left off last time? Before we dive into your main topic, could you share if there were any other things you’d like to cover today, or shall we focus entirely on the pool hall experience and that persistent feeling of being judged?
Hi. I'm... okay, I guess. Still thinking about that pool game a lot, to be honest. I think I'd like to focus on that—the feeling of being judged. It's been sticking with me longer than I expected.

That makes perfect sense; carrying the weight of that imagined judgment around is exhausting, so tackling it head-on seems like the most helpful path forward. Um... I'd say about a 7. Just thinking about it now, my shoulders are tensing up a little. I can almost see the table, and the faces of the other players watching me miss an easy shot.

Noticing those shoulders tense up is a very smart way to anchor yourself in the present moment before the story takes full control. Since you mentioned seeing the faces of the other players, can you describe what you imagine they are saying or thinking right now? Is it that familiar voice whispering "pathetic" again, or is there a different image forming?

Yeah, it's that word exactly — "pathetic." I can picture one guy rolling his eyes, and another giving this little smirk, like he knew I was going to mess up all along. It feels like they're all thinking, "What a loser, can't even sink a simple shot."

That "pathetic" script is incredibly vivid because it fits perfectly with your history of believing mistakes lead to humiliation. Let's run a quick experiment to test if that smirk and eye-roll are actually happening in front of you. Can you bring back the image of the pool hall on Friday, specifically focusing on the guy who missed an easy shot? I... I didn't really think about that. I mean, I was so focused on my own shot and my own miss. When I picture the other guy who messed up, nobody really reacted at all. They just waited for him to step back, and the game kept going. I guess I didn't notice that until now.

Since you noticed the tension rising in your shoulders and heard that word "pathetic," let's try applying that same "interrupt and relabel" technique we practiced. Instead of letting the image play out with the crowd reacting, could you take a deep breath and tell yourself, "This is just my brain adding a story, not what's actually happening"? How does introducing that phrase change the weight of the image in your mind?

I'll give it a try. *Takes a deep breath* "This is just my brain adding a story, not what's actually happening." Saying that... it feels a little lighter. Like a fog is clearing just a bit. The faces aren't as sharp, and the smirk doesn't seem as real as it did a minute ago.

Since you felt that lightening happen right after using that phrase, let's lock in that specific action for tomorrow: the next time you feel those shoulders tighten or hear "pathetic," you'll immediately whisper, "Just a story," to cut the power supply to the fear. I guess the main thing on my mind is that I messed up a small task yesterday because I wasn't focused, and now I'm scared that's the start of something bigger.

That sounds incredibly heavy to carry around, especially when a small mistake triggers such a large fear of consequences. And then this picture popped into my head of my manager calling me into a meeting and saying they've noticed my mistakes, and I just see myself getting let go. I think breaking that cycle is definitely the priority, because it's the part that keeps me from getting back on track.

That vivid picture of your manager and the immediate fear of being let go sounds terrifying, and it makes total sense why your stomach tightened up instantly; your body is treating that imagined scenario as a real emergency. Since we've identified that this catastrophic narrative is keeping you stuck, would you be willing to try a variation of the "emotion labeling" we discussed earlier, perhaps tailored specifically to this "being let go" story?

Just to make sure we're perfectly aligned, does slowing down long enough to simply state, "I am feeling terrified right now," before letting your mind race through the firing scenario feel like a manageable way to interrupt the loop for you?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It's just that when I'm in that moment, the fear feels so real that I almost don't want to slow down—like if I pause, it'll confirm that something bad is actually happening. But I guess if I just say "I am feeling terrified right now," it might stop the spiral from getting worse. I'm willing to give it a shot.

That hesitation is incredibly common and tells us the old belief system is still very strong, but your willingness to trust the "pause" button despite the fear is a huge sign of courage. Since you're ready to try this, let's solidify exactly what you'll do tonight: when you catch yourself seeing the "manager firing you" movie, stop for one second, breathe once, and say out loud, "I am feeling terrified right now," before letting your thoughts resume.

Before we finalize this, how does it land with you to just observe the knot in your stomach while speaking those words, and do you feel safe giving this a go for tonight?

I think I can manage that—observing the knot and just naming the feeling. It feels a bit strange, like I'm stepping outside of myself for a moment, but maybe that's exactly what I need. Yes, I feel safe enough to try it tonight, especially since I'll be at home and not at work.

That is a fantastic perspective; viewing the knot as an object you can observe rather than a command to act creates a wonderful gap between you and your anxiety. Since tonight is low-risk and allows for full reflection, please proceed with the plan: catch the "manager" image, pause, breathe, say the phrase out loud, and watch what happens to the knot and the rest of the spiral.

Before we wrap up, how does this specific script sound to you, and is there anything else you'd like to add or change about how we'll execute this tonight?

The script sounds clear and doable to me. I think I'll keep it simple and not overthink it—just pause, breathe, and say those words. I don't have any changes to suggest right now; I'm ready to give it an honest try tonight and see what happens.

That simplicity is exactly what matters most; stripping away the "why" and just focusing on the mechanical act of pausing and naming often cuts through the noise effectively. You are doing great work setting boundaries on your expectations and committing to an honest experiment regardless of the outcome.

Hello again, and thank you for showing up. On a scale of 1 to 10, how are you feeling today compared to last time? Also, before we dive into the main topics, I'd like to confirm our agenda for today: we can quickly touch on your recent struggle with the timer exercise, explore the "all-or-nothing" thoughts that seemed to block you, and then solidify a new, manageable plan for studying tonight. Does that outline sound good to you?

Hi. I'd say I'm at about a 4 or 5 today — maybe a little better than last time, but not by much. And yes, that agenda sounds fine. I'm still pretty stuck on that whole "if I can't get an A, what's the point" kind of thinking, so I guess that's the all-or-nothing part you mentioned.

Thank you for sharing that honest update—it’s clear you’re carrying that heavy “what’s the point” narrative, and it makes sense why your energy feels low when that mindset dominates. Since you’ve already identified the core pattern blocking you, let’s spend most of today testing whether that absolute standard holds up under scrutiny. As we look at that thought, does it feel helpful or helpful to you to keep holding onto it right now?

Honestly? Not helpful at all. It just makes me want to give up before I even try. But at the same time, it feels true — like if I'm not going to be at the top, then why bother putting in all that effort just to end up average?

It sounds like you're caught in a painful tug-of-war: logically knowing this thought is unhelpful, yet emotionally feeling that it's the only truth available to protect you from disappointment. That tension creates a lot of internal friction. Let's treat that feeling of "it feels true" as data rather than fact. If we look closely at the evidence supporting the idea that "average is worthless," what specific past outcomes do you recall where achieving an average result actually ruined your worth or future opportunities?

I guess... I can't really think of any specific time that happened. I mean, I've gotten B's before and I'm still here, still working toward my degree. But this feels different — like the midterm was a sign that I'm just not cut out for this program. I don't know, it's hard to separate the feeling from what's actually happened.

It makes perfect sense that you feel this way, especially after failing a midterm; your brain is trying to link that single event to a permanent lack of ability, which is why it feels so real. That leap from "one bad grade" to "I'm not cut out for this" is exactly where the distortion happens. Let's use some simple detective work here: if we assume that one setback meant you were fundamentally incapable of success, wouldn't that also mean you shouldn't have been admitted to the program in the first place? Can we see if that logic holds water given your history of getting Bs?

I guess you have a point. I did get in, and I did pass my first year classes. It's just... that midterm felt like proof that I've been fooling myself, you know? Like maybe I just got lucky before, and now reality is catching up. But when I really think about it, I did study for that exam, and I was confident going in. It just didn't turn out the way I expected.

That distinction is incredibly important—recognizing that you studied and prepared while admitting the outcome wasn't as hoped for shows you value your own effort, even though the result disappointed you. It seems like your brain is rewriting that preparation story to fit the "I'm not capable" narrative, treating the poor outcome as proof of wasted effort rather than just a statistical fluctuation. How does acknowledging that you did your best despite the disappointing result change the weight of that "reality catching up" feeling?

It... actually takes some of the sting out of it, I think. Because if I really was just faking it, I probably wouldn't have tried at all, or I would have just given up after the first bad grade. But I didn't. I studied, I asked for help, I made a schedule. So maybe it's not that I'm not capable — maybe I just hit a bump that I didn't see coming.

That is a powerful realization, and hearing yourself describe your own resilience—"studying, asking for help, making a schedule"—provides strong evidence that contradicts the idea that you are simply incapable. It shifts the narrative from a fixed flaw in your character to a temporary obstacle in your progress. Since we've gathered enough evidence to show that this "all-or-nothing" thought is a distortion rather than a fact, let's pivot to building a bridge across the gap. If the goal shifts from "perfect results to prove worth" to "making one small step toward mastery," does that feel like a safer, more manageable direction for tonight?

Yeah, I think it does. "One small step toward mastery" sounds a lot less terrifying than "ace everything or you're a failure." I guess I could try just reviewing the chapters I struggled with the most for maybe thirty minutes tonight, without worrying about getting a perfect score on a practice test. That feels... doable. Not great, but doable.

That is a wonderful reframing, and I love how you've connected it to your actual pain points—focusing on the chapters that hurt you most rather than trying to force perfection on the whole syllabus. By lowering the stakes to just "engagement with difficult material," you've removed the threat of failure that usually paralyzes you. Before we lock this in, I want to check your confidence level: if you commit to reviewing those tough chapters for thirty minutes tonight, on a scale of 0 to 10, how confident are you that you can actually sit down and start?

I'd say about a 7. The only reason it's not higher is because I'm still worried I'll get distracted or start feeling that "what's the point" feeling again. But if I just commit to the thirty minutes and don't think about the big picture, I think I can do it.

A seven is a very solid number, and identifying that distraction risk is actually a huge win because it turns a vague worry into a concrete variable we can watch. Let's lock in a specific protocol for tonight to handle that distraction: I suggest setting a visible timer for exactly thirty minutes, placing your phone in another room, and giving yourself permission to stop immediately if you feel overwhelmed, with the sole rule that you only need to open the book and read for those thirty minutes. Does that sound like a clear, safe plan for you to try tonight?

Yeah, that actually sounds really clear and safe. I like the idea of having a timer and putting my phone away — that way I'm not tempted to check it when things get hard. And knowing I can stop if I get overwhelmed makes it feel less like a test and more like... just an experiment. I'll try it tonight.

That shift from viewing it as a test to viewing it as a controlled experiment is brilliant and gives you the freedom to learn without the pressure of judgment. I'm really proud of how you've taken charge of designing a system that works for *you*, rather than forcing a rigid routine onto yourself. Since we have our plan locked in, how did the process of figuring out this new approach feel for you overall? Did finding a middle ground between "perfection" and "giving up" feel empowering, or was there any part of the journey that felt surprising or difficult?

It felt... weirdly freeing, honestly. Like I've been so stuck in that all-or-nothing mindset that I forgot there was a middle ground at all. The hardest part was admitting that maybe my first instinct — that I'm just not cut out for this — isn't the whole truth. But once I started looking at the evidence, like you said, it was harder to keep believing that story. I think I'm actually a little curious to see how tonight goes, which is not something I expected to feel.

It is beautiful to hear that you feel curiosity instead of dread—that's a massive cognitive shift in itself. Your willingness to stay present with the discomfort long enough to gather evidence shows real courage and self-awareness. I'd like to close by checking in on our relationship and the work we've done: how does our session feel overall for you today? Are there any aspects of our approach you'd like to tweak or any thoughts you have about how we can support each other even better moving forward?

I think today went really well. I came in feeling pretty down and unsure, and I'm leaving with an actual plan that doesn't feel impossible or terrifying. I appreciate that you didn't just tell me to think positively — you walked me through the evidence, and that made a bigger difference than I expected. I can't think of anything I'd change right now. I'm just grateful to have a way forward that doesn't feel like I'm setting myself up to fail.

That is such profound gratitude to receive, and I want to validate exactly what you noticed: the power of walking through the evidence together rather than just offering empty positivity. Recognizing that you built a plan based on your own strength and preferences, rather than mine, speaks volumes about your agency and trust in our partnership. Thank you for your honesty and for letting me witness that shift from paralysis to curiosity. I am so proud of the courage it took to face those feelings and find this middle path. We will meet tomorrow to debrief how those thirty minutes land, whenever you are ready. Have a wonderful evening, and remember: you are doing exactly what you need to do.

It makes perfect sense that you spiraled into "fraud" territory when the external validation didn't match your internal story; that gap between the sous chef's explanation and your belief confirms how powerful those automatic thoughts are when you're already anxious. Let's spend the next ten minutes unpacking that specific entry to see if we can find cracks in the "fraud" narrative, and then we'll brainstorm a quick grounding technique to handle that pre-rush knot.
