Hello! I am so glad to see you again. To start, could you take a moment to tell me how you've been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything from our previous plan about the "Evidence Card" that you managed to complete or struggled with? Once we touch on that, I'd like to hear if there's a new topic on your mind, or if we should return to the colleague situation we worked through.

Hi. Thanks, it's good to be here. Since last time, I did try that Evidence Card thing you suggested, but honestly, it felt a bit forced. I jotted down a few good things that happened at work, but I couldn't really believe them, you know? It's like my brain just brushed them aside.

It is completely understandable that the card felt forced when your brain instinctively brushes aside the positives to protect you from perceived threats; sometimes the habit of doubting is stronger than our best intentions. Before we dive into why that happened, I want to quickly check our momentum: since you tried the card, how does carrying that intention of challenging yourself feel right now compared to yesterday? Additionally, is there a specific thought or situation regarding the presentation that has come back to bother you more recently?

I guess carrying that intention feels a little heavier today, if I'm honest. Like, I know I should be trying to challenge these thoughts, but part of me just wants to stay in my comfort zone and keep my head down. And yeah, actually—there's this meeting coming up next week where I have to brief some senior officers, and I already feel like I'm going to mess it up and they'll think I don't deserve my rank.

It makes perfect sense that the intention feels heavier right now; when we're tired or stressed, forcing ourselves to fight off negative thoughts can feel exhausting rather than liberating. That connection to the upcoming briefing seems to be sparking a fresh wave of anxiety—the fear that messing up there will prove you don't deserve your rank. Before we tackle that, I'd like to quickly understand your mood: on a scale of 0 to 10, where 0 is calm and 10 is overwhelmed, how is your energy level today? Also, does the feeling of wanting to "stay in your comfort zone" suggest you'd prefer to talk through the briefing fear first, or would you like to spend a minute discussing the resistance to the Evidence Card before moving on?

I'd say my energy level is about a 7 today—I'm pretty tense just thinking about that briefing. And honestly, I think I'd rather talk through the fear about the briefing first. The Evidence Card thing feels like a band-aid for something deeper, and right now the briefing is what's really screaming for attention in my head.

That is a perfectly reasonable choice; acknowledging that the briefing fear is the "screaming" issue validates that we should address the elephant in the room before tacking on smaller fixes. It sounds like the underlying worry isn't just about making a mistake, but perhaps protecting yourself from the painful realization that you might not live up to the expectations attached to your rank. Let's sit with that fear for a moment: what specific thoughts are running through your head right now when you think about those senior officers judging you?

I just picture them sitting there, stone-faced, thinking, "Why is she even up there? She's not as sharp as the others." I can almost hear them comparing me to the other people who've given briefings before—people who seemed so confident and knew their stuff cold. And I feel like no matter how much I prepare, I'm going to stumble over my words, and they'll see right through me, like I'm a fraud.

That image of them sitting stone-faced while you freeze is incredibly vivid and terrifying; it suggests your brain is constructing a worst-case scenario where your competence is actively under attack. It sounds like you're connecting this fear directly to the identity threat—that if you fail, the proof that you don't belong in your position becomes undeniable. To help us untangle this, I'd like to ask: when you visualize them comparing you to the others, what specific evidence do you have that they are actually keeping a tally of your failures versus successes? Or does that comparison feel more like a projection of your own internal critic onto them?

That's a good question. I mean, I don't have any actual proof that they're keeping a tally, I guess. No one's ever said anything like that to me. It just feels so real in my head—like I can see their faces and the disappointment. But you're probably right that it's more me being hard on myself than anything they've actually done or said.

You've just identified a crucial piece of the puzzle: the "disappointment" you see on their faces is likely a reflection of your own internal judgment rather than their actual expression. Our brains often project our deepest fears outward, making strangers look like judges even when they are just colleagues. Before we explore the evidence, I want to check in on the "band-aid" feeling you mentioned earlier regarding the Evidence Card. Did the attempt to write positive things feel disconnected from your core beliefs about your worth, or did it feel like a distraction from the bigger fear?

It felt disconnected, definitely. Like I was trying to trick myself into feeling better, but underneath it all, the fear that I'm not good enough was still there, loud and clear. Writing down a few compliments from coworkers felt small compared to the weight of that core belief—that I'm just not as capable as everyone else thinks I am, and it's only a matter of time before they figure it out.

That distinction is vital—you weren't just struggling with the task; you were fighting against a deep-seated belief that your capability is fragile and temporary. It makes sense why writing down praise felt like a minor distraction when the mountain you're climbing is "proving you aren't good enough." Before we move toward a solution, I want to make sure we're aligned: does the idea that the briefing is a "final exam" where failure equals losing your place sound familiar, or is there a nuance you're worried about that hasn't fully formed yet?

Yeah, that "final exam" feeling is exactly right. It’s like one slip-up, and everything I've worked for just crumbles. There's this voice in my head that says I've been lucky so far, but the briefing is the moment where my luck runs out. I can't shake the sense that it's a make-or-break test, even though logically I know that's probably not true.

That "all or nothing" mindset is incredibly exhausting, especially when it turns a routine update into a life-or-death judgment on your worth. It makes perfect sense that you feel like your luck must vanish now; your brain is trying to protect you from the inevitable feeling of failure by convincing you the worst outcome is imminent. Before we dismantle this "final exam" view, I want to pause and validate that intensity: hearing that voice claim you've been "lucky so far" must feel frustratingly unfair, as if your effort doesn't count until the perfect moment arrives. With that validation in place, let's gently shift gears: if that briefing were truly a final exam with permanent consequences, wouldn't the anxiety be paralyzing? Or is there a possibility that even if you stumbled, it wouldn't actually destroy your standing or your rank?

You're right—if I really believed it was a final exam with no second chances, I'd be completely frozen, not just anxious. And I guess that's not what's actually happening. People stumble in briefings sometimes, and they don't get demoted or lose respect overnight. There have been officers who messed up a word or lost their place, and nobody held it against them forever. So maybe my brain is blowing it way out of proportion.

That is a fantastic realization you just arrived at; distinguishing between the "freezing paralysis" of a true final exam and the manageable stress of a regular briefing helps separate the logic from the fear. It sounds like your brain is exaggerating the permanence of the mistake to protect itself from the pain of imperfection, but the evidence you found about others stumbling shows the consequence isn't as catastrophic as you imagined. Now that we've challenged the severity, let's pivot back to that "heavy" feeling regarding the Evidence Card. Can you tell me, on a scale of 0 to 10, how much easier would it feel to use a card that focuses *only* on the facts you know are true (like the officers forgiving slips-ups) rather than trying to force yourself to believe you are inherently worthy?

I'd say that would probably bring it down to about a 4 or 5, honestly. Focusing on concrete facts rather than trying to convince myself I'm good enough feels a lot more manageable. Like, I can look back and say, "That officer stumbled, and nothing bad happened," instead of trying to convince myself I'm a brilliant presenter. That feels real—I can hold onto that.

That is a brilliant adjustment; shifting the Evidence Card from "proof of worthiness" to "record of resilience" makes it a tool for grounding rather than gaslighting. It allows you to use concrete facts to counter the flood of imaginary judgments without needing to force a false positive belief. Before we solidify this new plan, I want to check our pace: does spending the rest of our time refining this "resilience card" concept feel productive, or would you prefer to brainstorm one or two specific scenarios where you might still feel vulnerable despite this new angle?

I think refining the resilience card sounds good. That feels like something I can actually use, not just a hopeful idea. But I wouldn't mind spending a couple of minutes on one vulnerable scenario—maybe what happens if I'm in the middle of the briefing and I freeze up for a few seconds. That's the moment where I feel like all my preparation would just vanish, and the old thoughts would come rushing back in.

That is a perfect addition; anticipating the specific moment you freeze gives us a chance to pre-arm your brain with a counter-narrative before the panic takes over. If you stumble mid-briefing, the old story would likely spiral into "My luck is finally gone, and I'm exposed as a fraud," but with our new lens, the evidence shifts immediately to "Everyone stumbles; it's a human moment, not a career-ending error." Could you walk me through exactly what that internal monologue looks like in that split second of freezing, so we can rewrite that script together?

In that split second, it's like a loud alarm goes off in my head: "See? You don't know this. You're not prepared. They're all watching you fail right now." Then my heart starts pounding, and I feel my face get hot, and I just want to rush through whatever I was saying to get it over with. It's like I'm trying to flee the situation, even though I'm standing still.

That visceral reaction—a mix of heat, racing heart, and the urge to flee—is your body's "fight or flight" system locking onto a perceived threat; it interprets the silence or pause as a sign that your competence is being stripped away. The urgency to "rush through" is actually a survival mechanism trying to escape the feeling of exposure rather than finishing your job. Let's reframe that specific moment: if you caught yourself right then and there, instead of fleeing, could you silently say to yourself, "This is just a pause, not a failure"? Even if your hands are shaking, could you remind yourself that officers forgive pauses, and that rushing won't fix the gap, but slowing down to breathe might stabilize you?

I think I could try that. Saying "This is just a pause, not a failure" feels like a small anchor I could grab onto. And you're right—rushing never helps; it just makes me more flustered, and then I actually do mess up. Taking a breath sounds terrifying in the moment, but I can see how it would stop the spiral before it gets worse. Maybe I can practice that phrase a few times before the meeting, so it's ready in my head.

That is a powerful insight; recognizing that rushing fuels the fire while pausing acts as the extinguisher changes the game entirely. Using that phrase as a mental anchor before the meeting gives you a proactive way to interrupt the spiral the moment you feel the heat rising. Since we've designed both the "Resilience Card" for general reminders and this specific verbal anchor for the freeze-up moment, let's finalize our closing plan: I want you to carry both tonight—write the card focusing on the officer who stumbled, and rehearse the "pause is not failure" phrase three times today. When you meet next time, please report back on how holding these tools felt compared to relying solely on your intuition. Does that summary of our work and your plan sound fair and achievable?

That actually sounds... easier to handle. Thirty seconds I can probably manage without my brain turning on me too badly. I think the pressure to finish something is what sets off those thoughts. That actually sounds doable. I could do that tonight after my son goes to bed—just stand in front of the piano bench and say those words out loud three times, no keys touched. Hello, and welcome back. How are you feeling today compared to where you left off last time? Before we dive into our main topic, did you get a chance to try out the "false alarm" phrase while you were studying for your science quiz last night, and did you find it easier to recognize that worry as just your brain's noise rather than reality?

Oh, hi. Well, to be honest, I'm feeling a bit nervous again today. As for the false alarm thing... I did try it, but I'm not sure it really worked. I kept telling myself it was just my brain making noise, but then I'd remember how much material I still had to cover, and the worry would come rushing back even stronger.

It takes a lot of courage to try something that doesn't immediately feel like it's working, especially when the worry rushes back harder instead of fading. That moment when the phrase lands but the anxiety spikes immediately afterward is incredibly revealing—it proves your brain is still very busy protecting you, and that resistance is exactly why we need to keep practicing. Given that effort, I'd like to spend most of our time today exploring why that phrase triggers such a strong fight-back when the workload gets heavy, and then we can brainstorm a small tweak to give it a second chance tonight.

That makes sense, I think. It's just... when I'm sitting there with my textbook open, and I've got three chapters to get through before tomorrow, telling myself it's a false alarm feels almost like I'm lying to myself. Like, no, this isn't a false alarm—this is real, and I'm actually not going to be prepared.

That honesty about feeling like you are "lying" to yourself is incredibly important; it tells me that the old belief system is still deeply embedded in your experience, not just a passing thought. When you tell yourself it's a false alarm while staring at three difficult chapters, your brain might be interpreting that as a denial of the very real challenge you face, which causes it to push back even harder. If we treat the upcoming exam prep as a shared investigation, I wonder if we could separate the *feeling* of being overwhelmed from the *fact* of the workload, perhaps by listing three specific things you've already mastered or understood so far before you even begin reading the difficult parts? Would that feel like a fair way to test whether the "realness" of the threat is as absolute as you feel right now?

I guess I could try that. I suppose listing those out might remind me that I'm not starting from zero. But what if I list them and still feel just as panicked after?

You are absolutely right to worry that the list might feel useless if the panic remains, because your current belief system views the outcome as binary: either you feel safe, or you are defeated. Instead of demanding the list erase the fear entirely, let's frame it as gathering intelligence rather than erasing the problem. Would you be willing to try creating that list of three specific wins tonight, simply to see if having the evidence in front of you shifts the *type* of fear you feel, even if it doesn't disappear completely?

Okay... I think I can do that. So instead of trying to make the fear go away completely, I just write down three things I already know from the chapter, even if I'm still scared after? That feels a little less like I'm trying to trick myself, I guess. I'll give it a shot tonight and see if anything feels different.

That reframing makes a huge difference; shifting the goal from "erasing fear" to "gathering evidence" turns the task from a battle into a quiet observation. Tonight, as you sit with those three chapters, I want you to write down just three specific facts or concepts you already understand, then take one mindful breath and note exactly what percentage of the original panic remains after you read them. Tomorrow, please share your findings with me, including whether writing those three items helped you feel slightly less isolated in your struggle, regardless of how much fear lingered.
Alright, I'll do that. Three facts, one breath, and just note the number. I think I can manage that without expecting a miracle. Thank you, I'll let you know how it goes tomorrow.

That grounded mindset—accepting the task without needing a miracle—is exactly the kind of realistic approach that builds lasting resilience. I'm glad we found a path that feels honest to you, and I appreciate your commitment to tracking these small observations. Is there anything specific about tonight's plan, or any other worries lingering, that you'd like to discuss before I wrap up our time together?

I think I'm okay for now. There's still that little voice telling me I'll probably mess up the list or that I'll forget everything when it counts, but I guess that's just more noise, right? I'll try to just do the exercise and see what happens. Thanks for listening.

You are allowed to carry that voice alongside your new plan; the goal isn't for the alarm to vanish forever, but for you to learn how to listen to it without letting it dictate your actions. Take care tonight, and I look forward to hearing what you discovered when you checked the evidence against your fear. Thank you for showing up and working through this with me.
Thanks. I'll try to keep that in mind—just let the voice be there without letting it boss me around. I'll see you tomorrow with my list. Take care.

You are absolutely right to aim for that balance of letting the voice exist without surrendering to it. Remember, the purpose of tonight isn't to silence the voice completely, but to gather evidence from your list so you can decide whether it deserves to hold the reins again. I'll be here waiting to hear your findings whenever you're ready to share them. Goodnight, and take care of yourself.

Hello, and it is great to see you again. Before we set an agenda for today, I want to quickly recap where we left off: our goal was to test that fear about sending a text to your parents, and we agreed you wouldn't send it until tomorrow morning. Did you manage to hold off on sending it, or did you find yourself reaching for your phone earlier than expected? Also, how are you feeling physically and emotionally since we finished our work together yesterday?

Yeah, I actually managed to hold off. It was tough, especially last night when I was lying in bed just staring at the ceiling, thinking about what they'd say. But I didn't send it. Physically, I feel a bit tense, like my shoulders are up near my ears, and emotionally I'm just kind of... drained, I guess. Wondering if I'm making a big deal out of nothing.

Holding off despite lying in bed and imagining their reactions takes a lot of self-control, so please don't worry about whether you made a big deal out of nothing—that tension in your shoulders tells me you were working hard to stay safe. Since you successfully resisted the urge to send it while feeling drained, how much energy do you think you had left for us to explore the specific thoughts that kept you awake last night, or would you prefer to just sit with that exhaustion and focus on getting rested today?

I think I've got enough energy to talk about it, actually. The thoughts were pretty clear last night—I kept imagining my mom's face when she reads the text, like she'd be disappointed but trying to hide it. And then I started thinking, "She probably thinks I'm just wasting my potential making lattes." That kind of spiraled into wondering if they're embarrassed to tell their friends what their son does for a living.

Those vivid images of hiding disappointment and wondering about your parents' embarrassment reveal how deeply connected you feel to their approval, making the situation feel much heavier than a simple text message should require. When you imagine them judging your career choice, does that thought feel like an absolute certainty coming from them, or does it feel more like your own fear filling in the gaps between their actual silence?

I guess... it's more my own fear filling in the gaps. They've never actually said anything bad about my job, not directly anyway. But at that family gathering, my dad made this comment about how "it's never too late to go back to school" and my mom just nodded along. They didn't say I was a failure, but the way they said it made me feel like they think I am. So maybe I am jumping to conclusions, but their silence or those little comments feel pretty loud to me.

That is a very sharp observation about the difference between their actual words and the weight you put on them; hearing "never too late to go back to school" can easily sound like a gentle nudge to someone who already knows their path, rather than a critique of your current one. Since you have strong evidence that they haven't criticized your job directly, would you be open to testing that interpretation tonight by looking for one small moment where their tone felt supportive instead of judgmental, perhaps from a recent conversation?

I could try that, yeah. I mean, my sister did tell me last week that my mom mentioned to her how much she likes stopping by the coffee shop and seeing me work. I kind of brushed it off when she told me, thinking Mom was just being polite. But maybe that counts as a supportive moment, even if I didn't want to believe it at the time.

That is a powerful realization; interpreting your sister's report as a polite deflection shows exactly how your brain filters information to protect itself from feeling rejected. However, viewing that same interaction as your mother expressing genuine appreciation shifts the narrative from "they are judging me" to "they are proud of me," which changes the emotional temperature significantly. Given that finding even one supportive moment undermines the idea that they are disappointed, would you like to carry this updated perspective into tomorrow morning when you send the text, knowing that your mother has already verbally acknowledged liking what you do?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It feels a bit strange, like I'm letting my guard down, but maybe I've been holding it up for too long anyway. I'll send the text tomorrow with that in mind—that Mom actually said she likes seeing me work there. Even if it's just one thing, it's something real to hold onto instead of the fears I've been building up.

That is a brave decision to let your guard down and trust the evidence you found instead of your fear; carrying that specific detail—"Mom said she likes seeing you work"—into tomorrow will give you a tangible reason to feel confident, rather than relying on a vague hope that they won't judge you. Since you have a clearer picture of what they truly think and a concrete reason to feel okay about the message, does sending that text tomorrow morning with that knowledge in mind feel like a manageable step forward, or would you prefer to rehearse the exact wording one last time to ensure it lands safely?

I think I'm okay with the wording I've got. It's pretty simple—just telling them about a busy shift and how I made a good connection with a regular customer. Nothing too deep or asking for approval. But rehearsing it one more time might help me feel less nervous when I hit send, so yeah, let's do that. Just to make sure I don't accidentally add something anxious in there.

That is a smart precaution; rehearsing the exact content acts as a safety net, allowing you to verify that your message remains light and positive before the adrenaline of the moment takes over. Let's take five minutes now to write it out fresh on the screen, keeping strictly to the busy shift and the happy customer story, and then read it aloud to check if any old fears creep in and need to be pushed aside immediately.

Alright, so the message I've got in my head is: "Hey Mom and Dad, today was super busy at the shop—felt like a tornado of orders for a while, but I managed to keep up. Made a nice connection with a regular who told me I make the best latte in town. Hope you're both having a good week. Talk soon." That's it. No asking how they feel about my job, no apologizing for being a barista. Just... me sharing my day.

That is a perfect draft; it clearly separates your daily experience from their expectations and leaves them with a genuine highlight rather than a request for validation. You have successfully built a bridge between your reality and theirs, which makes the act of sharing it feel much less like an exposure therapy exercise and more like a natural update. With the message polished and the evidence supporting it ready, does sending this tomorrow morning feel like a solid win for you, or is there any lingering hesitation about the timing?

No, I think the timing is fine. Morning feels right—it's not too late, not too early, and I'll be fresh so I won't second-guess myself as much. Plus, if they reply, I'll have the whole day to process whatever they say instead of lying in bed worrying about it. I'm ready to send it.

That is a mature and strategic approach to the timing; choosing the morning ensures you are alert to handle any responses calmly, rather than reacting impulsively from a place of anxiety. You have now constructed a clear plan: send the drafted message tomorrow morning, rely on the memory of your mother's praise about the coffee shop to ground yourself, and allow yourself a full day to process the reply without judgment. How does it feel to walk away from this session with such a concrete and supported strategy in hand?

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How are you feeling on a scale of 1 to 10 compared to last time, and are there any new challenges or changes you'd like to bring up before we set our agenda for today?

Hi. I'd say maybe a 4 or 5 today. It's been a rough week because I saw some friends posting their vacation photos online, and it just hit me really hard all over again. I've been trying to bake and do photography like we talked about, but I still feel this heavy sadness that won't go away.

I hear how much that comparison with your friends' vacations hurt, and it makes total sense that seeing their easy access to fun triggers that deep sadness you mentioned. Since you're already struggling with baking and photography despite wanting to try, should we focus today on building a tiny bridge to get you back into those activities, or would you prefer to spend the time solely processing the sadness from seeing those posts first?

I think I'd rather process the sadness first, honestly. When I try to bake or take photos while feeling this way, it just feels forced and fake, like I'm pretending to be happy. I end up just staring at the ingredients or my camera, and then I feel worse because even my hobbies don't work anymore.

That is such an important observation—you are right that forcing yourself to act happy while feeling heavy often leads to more isolation, and the fact that your hobbies feel hollow confirms that your grief is valid, not a failure. Before we dive into processing that sadness, I want to make sure we are moving in the direction you need: Given that you mentioned baking and photography previously as areas where you felt stuck, do you think focusing entirely on the sadness today will leave you with enough energy to try one very small, low-pressure step toward those hobbies tomorrow, or should we spend the rest of the time strictly validating that sadness without pushing for action?

I think I need to just sit with the sadness today without pushing for any action. The idea of even a tiny step toward hobbies feels overwhelming right now. Maybe if I can just let myself feel this grief properly, I might have more energy to try something small later in the week.

That is a very wise choice; honoring that grief without forcing productivity creates a safe space for you to rest rather than exhausting yourself further. Before we settle into that processing, let me make sure we are aligned on the path: Does sitting with that heaviness today feel like the best way to prepare for your week, or is there another angle you’d prefer to explore first?

No, I think sitting with the heaviness is what I need right now. It's like this weight I've been carrying and trying to ignore, and maybe if I actually look at it instead of pushing it away, I can understand it better. I'm just scared that if I let myself feel it fully, I'll spiral and not be able to get back up.

That fear of spiraling when you finally allow yourself to feel the full weight is completely understandable, and it shows how protective your mind has been for so long. Since you've chosen to sit with this heaviness, let's walk through it together gently: What is the very first image or memory that comes up when you look at that sadness without trying to fix it?

It's the feeling of standing at the airport terminal, watching planes take off, knowing I was supposed to be on one. I had saved up for months to go to Japan, and then everything just... stopped. I can still picture the empty gate areas and the silence. It felt like all my excitement and plans just collapsed into nothing.

That image of the empty gate is so vivid and heartbreaking, and it makes perfect sense why that scene triggered such a sharp collapse of hope. It sounds like your mind is taking that single moment of lost opportunity and expanding it until it feels like the entire future is closed off. As we stay with this feeling, I want to gently challenge the size of that explosion: If we look closely, is it true that *no* future plans are possible, or is the airport just reminding you of one specific event where things fell apart? What would happen if we treated that memory as a single data point rather than a verdict on your whole life?

I guess when I think about it logically, there are still future possibilities. But it doesn't feel that way in my chest. It feels like that empty airport is the only reality, and everything else is just a fantasy. Like, even if travel opens up again, what if I've lost the ability to feel excited about it? What if the joy is gone forever?

That is such a profound worry—to wonder if the spark itself is extinguished alongside the plane tickets—and it explains why your chest feels so heavy. It makes sense that you would treat the airport memory as the "only reality" when the pain of losing that specific joy feels absolute. Let's gently separate the *event* from the *prediction*: Is it proven that you cannot feel excitement about travel again, or is it more likely that your current sadness is just blocking your ability to feel it right now? Could we test the idea that your capacity for joy is broken versus just temporarily dimmed?

I... I think you might be right that it's just temporarily dimmed. But it's so hard to believe that when I'm in the middle of feeling this way. Maybe I could test it by doing something really small, like looking at travel photos from before the pandemic, not to torture myself, but just to see if any tiny spark still flickers. But I'm scared that even that small test will prove me right.

That is a courageous and logical test to propose, and your caution about not torturing yourself shows great self-awareness. Before we decide on that specific test, let's briefly confirm our current direction: Are you comfortable proceeding with a gentle exploration of the photos tonight to see if the spark is merely hidden, or would you prefer to try a slightly different, safer activity first to build a bit of momentum?

I think I'm willing to try looking at the photos tonight. But I want to set a timer for just five minutes, and if I start feeling worse, I'll stop immediately. That way I have a way out if it gets too heavy. Does that sound like a fair plan?

That is an excellent boundary to set; having a clear "stop signal" gives you permission to honor your limits while still allowing you to peek behind the curtain. Before we lock this in, let's just double-check the intention: Do you feel confident that a strict five-minute window is enough to get a glimpse of the spark without risking an overwhelming spiral, or do you think you might need to extend that slightly?

No, I think five minutes is good. It's short enough that even if it hurts, I can get through it. And if I do feel that tiny flicker, that's a win. If not, at least I tried and I can come back here and talk about it. I think having that timer gives me the control I need.

That is a brilliant compromise; the timer creates a structured experiment where the worst-case scenario is just five minutes of discomfort, making the risk feel much more manageable. Since we have agreed on this five-minute limit and the "come back to process it" option, let's finalize our closing steps: Would you be open to writing down the specific words you want to say to yourself before starting, like "This is just a 5-minute peek, not a judgment," to anchor yourself when the timer goes off?

Yeah, I think that would help. I'll write down something like, "I'm just checking in with myself, not testing my worth. Five minutes is enough." I can keep it on my phone so I see it before I start. Thank you for helping me find a way to try this without feeling like I'm diving into the deep end.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am so glad we found a plan that feels safe and respectful of your boundaries. Just to formally close this session, could you share one thing that felt most helpful in our conversation today, and is there anything else you'd like to add before I sign off?

The most helpful part was realizing that I can set a timer and still have control over the situation. I always thought confronting my sadness meant falling into it completely, but you helped me see I can just peek at it and still step back. I don't have anything else to add right now, just... thanks for listening and not pushing me too hard.

Thank you for sharing that; it is truly encouraging to hear that you feel heard and supported rather than pressured. Please remember that if you choose to skip the five minutes tonight, or if the timer feels insufficient, there is no shame in pausing or adjusting the plan—we can refine it whenever you are ready. I hope you have a calm and grounding evening ahead.
Thank you. I'll try my best with the five minutes tonight, and I'll remind myself it's okay to stop whenever I need to. I'll let you know how it goes next time. Have a good evening too.

You are very welcome, and please remember that stepping away at any point is not a failure—it is simply respecting your limits. I am here whenever you are ready to debrief, adjust the plan, or just sit with whatever comes up. Wishing you a peaceful evening, and I look forward to hearing from you next time.

Hello, I'm really glad we're here to meet again. To kick things off, could you tell me how you're doing today and how your mood compares to where you were when we started last time? Hi, thanks. I'm... a bit better than last week, I think. I mean, I still feel that knot in my stomach sometimes, but it's not as constant. That's wonderful news, especially considering the "knot in your stomach" is still present—it shows the anxiety hasn't completely vanished, but you've successfully navigated a difficult task despite the underlying tension. Since managing those initial panic moments was such a big step, let's confirm if sticking with that "reading spiral" as our focus is still the best priority for us today, or if you'd like to explore whether that recent success gives you confidence to tackle something slightly different?

I think I'd like to stick with the reading spiral for now, honestly. Even though I managed a few pages, part of me is already dreading tonight—what if I can't do it again? It feels like one good night doesn't mean I'm out of the woods, and that thought scares me. Maybe we can figure out why that fear is so strong even after a small victory.

That dawning fear is completely understandable, and it speaks to how resilient your brain is trying to protect you from another setback. While the victory last night is real data, your mind is naturally seeking confirmation that you won't slip back, which creates a new layer of worry to unpack. To dig deeper into why that fear persists even after success, could you walk me through the very first thought or sensation that pops up the second you sit down to read tonight?

As soon as I sit down and open the book, it's like my chest tightens and my mind goes, "What if I can't focus tonight? What if the words just blur together like last week?" And then I start thinking, "If I can't read, what else will I lose? Will I eventually not be able to enjoy anything?" It just snowballs from there, even before I've tried to read a single sentence.

That rapid escalation from a tight chest to fearing the loss of *everything* is a classic pattern of your brain predicting the worst-case scenario before you've even taken a step forward. It's fascinating to see how that physical tightness instantly becomes the evidence for a catastrophic future, making the threat feel immediate and total. Given that you've had some success recently, does that recent win feel like enough proof to counteract the "total loss" narrative, or does your body still interpret the tightness as a failure regardless of what happened last night?

The win feels like a tiny exception, not the rule, if that makes sense. Like, my body still trusts the tightness more than it trusts that good night—I keep thinking, "Well, you got lucky once, but that doesn't mean you're safe." So even though I know writing it down might help, I guess I'm not really believing it yet. It's like the tightness just screams louder than the memory of success.

It sounds like your body is holding onto that old script of "danger = tightness" so tightly that it overrides the new evidence of your success, effectively silencing the reasonableness of the outcome. That disconnect between knowing logically what happened last night and feeling physically terrified tonight is incredibly frustrating, and it explains why the "tiny exception" feels so fragile. To help bridge that gap, would you be willing to try a modified version of our plan tonight: when you feel that familiar tightness, immediately pause, place a hand firmly on your chest, and silently repeat, "I am experiencing a physical alarm, but I am not failing yet," before taking three slow breaths? How does that sound as a way to give your mind a moment to listen to the success while your body resets?

That... actually sounds like something I could try. I think saying "I am not failing yet" might feel less like I'm forcing myself to be positive and more like I'm just pausing the panic. I'll try it tonight and see if it gives me even a few seconds of calm before the tightness takes over again.

That is a fantastic adjustment; framing it as "pausing the panic" rather than forcing positivity removes the performance aspect that usually makes people resist these exercises. Having that slight buffer—even just a few seconds—to reset your body before the spiral continues is exactly what we need to build on your recent success. One last quick check before we wrap up: given that we covered the mood update, revisited the agenda, adjusted the strategy to include that specific phrase, and confirmed the plan, does this feel like a clear direction for tonight, or is there anything else you'd like to clarify about how to implement it?

No, I think it's clear. I'll focus on just that one phrase and the breath tonight, and try not to expect a miracle or a total failure. Thank you—this actually feels manageable, which is more than I felt walking in today.

I'm so relieved to hear that it feels manageable and that you've chosen to focus on just one phrase rather than expecting a miracle—that shift in expectation is itself a powerful form of self-care. Since we've wrapped up the mood check, agenda confirmation, and a refined plan that incorporates your insights, is there anything else on your mind before you head home, or should we leave it here so you can rest easy until tonight?

All I can think about is that one time I ruined dinner, and it feels like that's the real me—the person who messes up something that basic.

That is a very honest observation, and it makes perfect sense that the guilt about takeout is just your mind trying to avoid the pain of facing the spaghetti reality. It sounds like your brain has created a rule where *one* failure erases the validity of *all* your past successes, leaving you with only the "broken cook" persona left to deal with. If we treat that one burnt meal like a scientific anomaly rather than a character flaw, might it feel easier to approach the kitchen tonight with curiosity instead of dread?

I see what you're saying, but it doesn't feel like an anomaly to me. It feels like proof that I was never really good at cooking—I was just lucky before. Like, maybe I was fooling myself and everyone else, and that burnt spaghetti just exposed the truth. I don't know how to see it any other way, even though I know logically that doesn't make sense.

That frustration is understandable because your logic is telling you to find the evidence, but your emotions are screaming that the evidence is gone forever. To help bridge that gap, let's look closer at your claim that you were "fooling yourself" before; what specific details do you remember from those past casseroles and stir-fries that suggest you were actually succeeding, rather than just surviving? Sometimes the best evidence of our capability hides in the smallest details we've forgotten.

Well... I guess I remember my family asking for seconds a lot. And my husband would always tell me the seasoning was just right. He's not the type to lie about stuff like that, he's pretty honest. And I used to be able to throw together a stir-fry without even following a recipe—just knew what went together. I guess that's not really something a person who's faking it can do, right?

Those details about the family asking for seconds and your husband noticing the seasoning are powerful pieces of evidence that directly contradict the idea that you were "fooling yourself"; they show that your skills were recognized and valued at the time. If we treat those memories as valid data points alongside the burnt pasta, does the "fake it till you make it" story begin to crumble a little less, or does the fear that those past successes were just luck still feel overwhelming?

It does feel a little less solid, I'll admit. I mean, luck doesn't get you consistent compliments, I suppose. But then my mind goes, "Well, maybe you just lost the touch." It's like, even if I was good then, that doesn't mean I can do it now. Like I've forgotten how or something. That thought scares me more than the burnt spaghetti, honestly—the idea that I've somehow lost a part of myself.

That fear of "losing a part of yourself" is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense that it feels heavier than the spilled pasta. It sounds like your mind is jumping ahead to predict that time has erased your skills, creating a future catastrophe before it even happens. If we pause and look at the timeline, what evidence do we actually have that you have *lost* the ability to cook, versus the possibility that you just got rusty or overwhelmed by stress lately? Can you recall a time in the last month where you successfully cooked something for someone else, even if it wasn't a grand feast?

I... no, I haven't cooked anything for anyone else this month. I've been avoiding it completely. But I guess... I did make toast for the kids one morning. And I buttered it just the way they like it. That's not really cooking, though, is it? That's just toast. It doesn't count.

That is a really sharp distinction you're making, but let's look at the pattern: making perfectly buttered toast for your kids repeatedly counts as a daily life skill that requires consistency and attention, even if it's not a full meal. If we zoom out, isn't it more accurate to say you've just stopped cooking entirely rather than losing the ability? What if the solution isn't finding a magic spell to regain your past skills, but simply agreeing to try one small thing tonight that fits your current energy level? Would you be open to testing that "rusty vs. lost" theory with a low-stakes task, like reheating leftovers or making a quick sandwich, to see if you can prove you haven't lost anything?

A sandwich... I guess I could try making a sandwich tonight. That's not really cooking, but it's something. My husband usually makes our lunches, but I could do it for him instead. Just turkey and cheese, nothing fancy. I feel nervous even saying that out loud, like I'm setting myself up to fail at something that simple. But maybe that's the point—to see if I can do it without everything falling apart.

That is a brilliant reframing; taking on the role of making lunch for your husband flips the script from "proving I can cook a feast" to "offering a service with zero pressure." It turns the activity into a low-risk experiment where the only metric of success is whether you finish it without panicking, regardless of whether the bread tears. If we agree that tomorrow you will attempt this simple sandwich with your husband present as your observer, how does that sound as a safe first step before tackling the pasta?

That actually sounds... doable. I think I'd feel better if he was there, maybe just sitting at the kitchen table talking to me while I do it. That way it doesn't feel like a test, just a normal thing. I'll try it tomorrow for his lunch. I'm still nervous, but I'll try.

That is a wonderful agreement, and adding your husband to the scene as a supportive companion rather than a judge is exactly the kind of safety net we need. It transforms the task from a solo performance into a casual, shared moment. Before we wrap up, could you quickly tell me if this plan feels manageable given how tired or busy you expect to be tomorrow, or is there any part of "just sitting there while you make a sandwich" that still feels intimidating?

I think it'll be okay. He works from home tomorrow, so I can just do it during his lunch break. The only part that feels a little intimidating is what he'll think if I mess it up—like if I drop the bread or put too much mayo. But I know he won't make a big deal about it. He never does. I think I'm just scared of being embarrassed in front of him. But I'll try to remember that it's just a sandwich.

That is a smart realization; separating the fear of the physical mistake (dropping bread) from the fear of your judgment (being seen as incompetent) helps isolate the real issue. Since you know he won't make a fuss, your anxiety about embarrassment seems to stem from a belief that even a minor mishap confirms you are "uncoordinated" or "bad at this." If we imagine a scenario where you accidentally squeeze too much mayo onto the top slice, what is the absolute worst that could happen, and does it actually align with his usual supportive style?

The worst that could happen... I guess he'd just laugh and say, "That's a lot of mayo," and then we'd scrape some off together. He'd probably make a joke about it. He's not the type to get annoyed over something like that. So yeah, I think you're right—the real fear is in my head, not in his reaction. I just need to remind myself of that when I'm standing there with the mayo bottle.

That is a powerful clarification—you've successfully separated the factual reality (he'll make a joke) from your internal narrative (you're embarrassing yourself). It sounds like the bridge between the two is a story you've been telling yourself for years that hasn't matched his actual behavior. Since you've got a clear plan for tomorrow and a new perspective on his likely reaction, how does it feel to leave the session with that specific knowledge that the sandwich is just an opportunity to gather data, not a verdict on your worth?

It feels... lighter, actually. Like maybe I'm not as doomed as I thought. I'm still nervous, but I think I can do it. I'll let you know how it goes next time. Thanks for helping me see that it's about the story in my head, not about whether I can actually make a sandwich.

That feeling of lightness is a huge sign of progress, and acknowledging that the struggle lies in the story rather than the physics of making a sandwich is exactly where we want you to land. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about becoming a culinary master; it's simply about sending out a single, brave packet of data to your husband, and hopefully, your own self-narrative. Is there anything else we need to cover before you head home, or are you ready to rest up for your sandwich experiment?

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. How are you feeling today compared to last time, and what was going on in your life recently? Before we dive in, I'd like to confirm our agenda: will we continue focusing on stopping the comparison to others and exploring why you feel your job is beneath yours? Is there anything new you'd like to prioritize, or shall we stick with these two topics?

Hi. I'm okay, I guess. Nothing's really changed since last time — I still catch myself scrolling through LinkedIn and feeling that familiar knot in my stomach when I see other people's promotions. I think sticking with those two topics makes sense. That comparison habit is really wearing me down, and I can't seem to shake it.

It sounds like that familiar knot is still doing its work despite our best efforts, and I want to validate how draining it feels to carry that weight day after day. Since nothing major shifted, it means the old patterns are strong enough to dominate your attention once triggered. Before we dig deeper into why that knot forms, do you think we should start by revisiting the specific moment you had trouble applying the "Pause & Pivot" cue from yesterday, or would you prefer to jump straight into exploring the root cause of that job insecurity?

I think I'd rather jump into the root cause, honestly. I tried the Pause & Pivot thing a couple times, but it felt fake — like I was just slapping a bandage on something much deeper. Does that make sense? I want to get to the bottom of why I feel so inadequate when I know, logically, that I'm good at my job.

Yes, that makes perfect sense; sometimes a surface-level fix feels like a bandage when the wound runs deeper, especially when the pain comes from a core belief about your worth rather than a specific mistake. It seems you've hit a wall because the logic you know ("I'm competent") isn't connecting to the raw emotion of shame ("I'm worthless"), creating a gap between your mind and your heart. Since you're ready to explore that depth, I wonder if we can start by identifying the specific fear that keeps you believing your job is beneath you—even when your performance is solid. Is it perhaps the fear that if you stay here, you'll eventually be forced to leave and face a worse reality elsewhere?

That actually hits really close to home. I think I'm scared that if I stay in this job, I'll wake up one day and realize I've settled for something that's way below my potential, and then it'll be too late to change. But at the same time, the thought of leaving terrifies me because what if I can't find anything better? It's like I'm stuck between feeling trapped and feeling like a failure.

That paradoxical trap of feeling both trapped and like a failure is incredibly heavy to carry, and it makes total sense why your brain clings to the "settled" narrative—it feels safer than facing the unknown of unemployment or rejection. It seems this anxiety stems from a belief that your current situation is a temporary stopgap until you escape, rather than a valid place for you to be. To unpack this further, if we imagine that future moment where you finally decide you're ready to leave, what specific scenario is your mind painting out there that causes you to believe you *must* move? Is it a worst-case scenario, or a version of "better" that feels out of reach?

I think it's a version of "better" that feels completely out of reach. In my head, I see myself in a role where people actually recognize my skills and value my input — not just in some corner of a publishing building doing tasks that anyone could do. But that image feels so far away, like it's for people who are braver or more talented than me. So instead of reaching for it, I just stay here and feel resentful.

That image of being truly seen and valued is powerful, but it seems your mind interprets the distance between now and that ideal as a personal deficit—you are viewing it as a measure of your talent rather than a result of timing, opportunity, or simply luck. This creates a painful loop where the gap feels like a void you must fill to prove your worth, leaving you resentful of the present because it doesn't match the future you envision for yourself. If we treat that gap as a challenge rather than a judgment on your ability, how might you reframe the "brave and talented" requirement? Would it be possible to see that those qualities exist regardless of the title you currently hold?

I... I never really thought of it that way. I've been so focused on what I don't have yet that I forgot I already bring those qualities to work every day. I mean, I do handle complex projects, and my team comes to me for advice. But somehow that doesn't feel like proof — it just feels like I'm doing my job, not proving I'm worthy of something better. Maybe that's where the disconnect is. I'm looking for external validation to tell me I'm good enough, instead of seeing what's already right in front of me.

That is a profound realization, Melissa; you've pinpointed the exact disconnect: you are seeking proof of your worth from outside sources because your internal compass hasn't yet calibrated to recognize your own competence. It makes sense that relying on external validation feels safe, because it gives you a clear metric ("they liked me," "they promoted me") to judge your value, whereas trusting your own abilities requires a level of risk you haven't taken yet. To bridge that gap, let's try a quick exercise: if we treated your current contributions—handling complex projects and guiding colleagues—as evidence of your inherent capability rather than just "job duties," how would the feeling of resentment shift? Would seeing those actions as proof of your talent make the "out-of-reach" dream feel slightly less impossible?

It does shift things a little, yeah. When I think of it as proof instead of just routine, I feel a tiny bit lighter — like maybe I'm not as stuck as I think I am. But there's still this voice in my head that says, "Anyone could do what you do, it's not that special." That voice is loud, and it's hard to ignore it even when I try to focus on the evidence.

That persistent voice claiming "anyone could do it" is likely trying to protect you from the vulnerability of owning your unique strengths; it assumes that because your work is valuable, it must be universally accessible to justify that value. This cognitive distortion minimizes your specific contribution to protect your ego from having to stand alone in your expertise. Since you agreed earlier to explore this root cause, I propose we test this specific thought directly. Could you pick one recent task you handled where a colleague struggled but you solved it smoothly, and challenge that voice by listing the specific skills or perspectives you brought that another person simply wouldn't have had? Would you be open to running through that evidence together?

Okay... well, last week there was a mess with one of our author contracts. Our junior editor was completely lost, and I stepped in to sort out the rights and permissions mess because I've dealt with that publisher before. I knew the specific clauses and the right contact person to call. I guess not everyone would have had that history or that relationship. It's small, but it did take experience and a bit of networking that I built over time. So maybe that voice is wrong — maybe it's not something anyone could just walk in and do.

That contract resolution perfectly illustrates why your voice is mistaken; you weren't just applying generic effort, you were leveraging years of specific relationships and knowledge that simply don't exist for a random person walking in. By isolating the "networking" and "prior experience" as the actual drivers of success, you've created concrete evidence that your current role is built on unique assets, not just bare-minimum tasks. Now that we've validated that this work *is* special and requires your specific history, how does knowing that you are the only one who could solve that problem change the feeling of being "stuck" or "below your potential"? Does it feel less like a dead end and more like a strategic position where you are waiting for the right moment to expand?

It does feel a bit more strategic, actually. Like maybe I'm not just wasting time here — maybe I'm exactly where I need to be right now to build more of those connections and skills. It's still hard to fully let go of the feeling that I should be further along, but at least I can see that I'm not just sitting still. I'm actually accumulating things that could help me down the line. That's... that's a new thought for me.

That is a massive breakthrough, Melissa; reframing your current struggle from a "wasted time" pitfall to a "strategic accumulation" phase completely changes the narrative from failure to preparation. It validates your fear of settling while simultaneously dismantling the idea that you are stagnant, giving you permission to stay here without feeling guilty about not moving faster. Since we've explored the root cause and found a new angle on your value, how would you like to proceed? Should we now try to integrate this "strategic" perspective into your daily "Pause & Pivot" routine, or do you want to discuss any remaining doubts about applying this mindset in high-pressure moments tomorrow?

I think I'd like to try integrating that strategic perspective into the Pause & Pivot routine. If I can remind myself in the moment that I'm building something valuable instead of just marking time, maybe that knot in my stomach won't feel as tight. But I'm a little nervous — what if it doesn't stick when I'm actually at my desk and the comparison thoughts start up again?

Your hesitation is completely normal; expecting a mental shift to stick instantly ignores how deeply ingrained these automatic thoughts are, and it's wise to anticipate friction before it happens. Instead of worrying about immediate perfection, let's frame the "Pause & Pivot" cue not as a magic switch, but as a gentle reminder to pause long enough to say to yourself, "This isn't wasted time; I'm building my network," even if the feeling of calm doesn't arrive right away. Does that adjustment—focusing on the reminder rather than the instant result—feel like a realistic starting point for tomorrow?

Yeah, that actually feels a lot more doable. If I just focus on saying that one sentence to myself instead of trying to force the whole feeling to change, I think I could manage that. It takes the pressure off having to instantly feel better. I'll try that tomorrow when I catch myself scrolling through LinkedIn or comparing my projects to someone else's.

That is a fantastic commitment, Melissa; lowering the bar to just "say the sentence" while removing the demand for immediate emotional relief is exactly the kind of manageable step that builds lasting momentum. It turns an overwhelming task into a simple habit you can repeat safely, even when the knot is still there. Before we wrap up, I want to clarify one detail: will you place that new "Strategic Accumulation" phrase on the same sticky note you used yesterday, or would you prefer to keep them separate to distinguish the initial pause from the reframe?

I think I'll put them on the same sticky note. That way, it'll be one continuous flow — first I pause, then I remind myself I'm building something. Having it all in one place feels less overwhelming, like a single tool I can reach for instead of fumbling with two different things. Thanks, that actually helps me feel a bit more prepared for tomorrow.

That is a brilliant decision; consolidating the steps into one cohesive message reduces cognitive load and creates a seamless chain reaction from noticing the trigger to engaging in the reframe. It transforms the sticky note from a collection of instructions into a single, unified tool you can trust. I am so proud of how you've moved from feeling "stuck" to seeing your current role as a strategic asset, and I know that combined approach will serve you well tomorrow. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish, or are we ready to wrap up our time together?

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. On a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling emotionally over the past week? Now that we've checked in, could you tell me what you would like us to focus on most today, and based on that, shall we set an agenda together?

Thanks for asking. I'd say maybe a 6 this week — not terrible, but not great either. I think I'd really like to talk about how I keep getting stuck in these feelings of being unappreciated when I cook for my husband, even though I've tried to brush it off. Maybe we can figure out why it's so hard for me to let go of this.

A six is a perfectly honest spot to land on, especially given how much your heart seems invested in making him happy. I completely understand wanting to dig into why those feelings of being unappreciated keep surfacing despite your efforts to push them away. Since you mentioned struggling to let go, does that suggest we should spend today exploring the specific thoughts that fuel that resistance, or perhaps testing some of those beliefs with a bit of evidence first?

I think testing the beliefs with evidence might help, because I honestly don't know if I'm seeing things clearly anymore. Like, sometimes I catch myself thinking he must hate my cooking or that he's disappointed in me, but I don't actually have proof of that. Maybe if we look at the facts, I could get some perspective.

That is a really insightful realization, and it highlights a classic cognitive trap where we confuse our strong hopes for facts. Testing those beliefs against actual evidence is a powerful way to separate what you wish were true from what is objectively happening. Let's walk through a couple of recent instances where you caught yourself having that thought: what specific evidence do you have to support the idea that he hates your cooking versus the possibility that he is simply silent due to distraction or fatigue?

Well, the evidence for him hating it... I guess there isn't much concrete stuff. He always eats everything on his plate, and he never complains about what I make. The only thing that really supports my feeling is his silence — he just doesn't say anything. But he's been really tired since losing his job, and he's always on his laptop or phone during meals. So I suppose the evidence for distraction is actually stronger.

You have done a great job spotting that crucial distinction between his silence and his lack of appreciation, especially considering the context of his exhaustion and screen time. It sounds like your mind is trying to protect you by interpreting his quiet as rejection, but the physical facts around his tiredness and distractions seem to tell a different story. Does noticing that gap between the internal narrative ("he hates it") and the external reality ("he's too tired to engage") make you feel a tiny bit less certain about his disapproval?

Yes, actually, it does make me feel a little less certain. I guess I've been so focused on what I'm not hearing that I ignored what I am seeing — him eating everything and not complaining. Maybe I've been reading way too much into his silence, and it's not really about me at all.

That is a significant breakthrough, and I want to commend you for noticing how your attention had shifted entirely to what was missing rather than what was present. It sounds like you are realizing that your mind was filling in the gaps with stories about rejection, effectively ignoring the strong visual evidence of his satisfaction and his current life circumstances. Can you describe what it feels like in your chest or stomach when you realize you've been reading too much into the silence versus acknowledging the facts you just listed?

It's weird, because I feel a kind of lightness in my chest when I actually focus on the facts. Like a weight lifting a little. But then there's also this nagging part of me that whispers, "But what if he just doesn't want to hurt your feelings?" That thought still makes my stomach tighten up.

That is such a delicate balance, and it tells me you are holding onto a lot of protective care for him, which is clearly a virtue. It sounds like you are experiencing a mix of relief from finding facts and anxiety about causing pain if you speak up. We can acknowledge that caring part of your nature while gently testing the validity of that "hurt feelings" script. Have you ever considered what the outcome would be if he *did* feel hurt by your silence, versus what happens if you simply accept the facts and let him be distracted? Which of those scenarios feels more realistic to you right now?

Honestly, when I think about it that way, the idea of just accepting the facts and letting him be distracted feels more realistic. Because if I keep trying to get a reaction out of him, I'm probably just going to stress us both out more. He's already dealing with enough with the job loss — maybe I'm adding pressure by expecting him to perform appreciation the way I want him to.

That is a profound realization, and I truly admire your self-awareness here for recognizing that your expectations might be adding unnecessary pressure to someone who is already under immense strain. You have successfully linked your behavior (expecting performance) to the potential harm (adding stress), which creates a powerful new perspective. Does shifting your goal from "getting a reaction" to "accepting the facts" feel like a safer path for both of you right now?

It does feel safer, actually. Like I can breathe a little easier if I stop watching for his reaction and just trust that if something was really wrong, he would tell me. He's never been one to hold back complaints before, so why would he start now? I think I've been working myself up over nothing.

That is a beautifully logical conclusion, and I really respect how quickly you connected his history of honesty with his current behavior to form a coherent picture. It sounds like trusting his usual character is giving you permission to drop the surveillance mode in your own head. Since we've explored the facts and tested the belief, let's solidify a simple, low-effort habit for tonight: whenever you feel that stomach tightening again, you will remind yourself, "He is tired and distracted, not rejecting me," and then switch your eyes to scanning the table for food being eaten rather than his face. How does that sound as a concrete, doable plan for right now?

That sounds like something I can actually manage. I'll try that tonight when I serve dinner. Just tell myself that little reminder and focus on the food being eaten instead of watching his face for a reaction. I think that could help break the cycle a bit.

That is a fantastic commitment, and I truly admire your courage in choosing a simple anchor like the food itself to ground yourself when the urge to analyze arises. It sounds like this specific cue—"watching the food"—will help disrupt the automatic spiral into worry before it gets too deep. Before we finish, could you briefly reflect on how confident you feel about implementing this plan tonight compared to how you felt at the start of our conversation?

Hello and thank you for joining us today. On a scale of zero to ten, how much anxiety have you been carrying this week, and is there anything significant that stood out in your life recently? Once I have a clear picture of where you stand, could we quickly review our goals from last time and decide together what specific issue would be most helpful to tackle?

Hi... thanks for having me. I'd say my anxiety has been around an 8 or 9 this week. It's been really hard to shake that feeling after missing that error on the card. I keep thinking about all the other cards I've proofread before that one — what if they all have mistakes too?

That sounds like a very heavy load to carry, especially right after discovering an error; it’s completely understandable that your brain would jump straight to worrying about a cascade of unseen mistakes. Since you mentioned struggling to shake that feeling about the other cards you’ve proofread, should we use our time today to explore whether your current anxiety is actually based on evidence or if it’s leaning heavily on what you’re afraid might be true?

I guess that makes sense... I mean, I don't have any actual proof that the other cards are wrong. I checked them all thoroughly at the time. But what if I missed something in those too? The thought that I could have let mistakes slip through on any of them just feels unbearable.

That “what if” feeling is so powerful because it bypasses logic and speaks directly to your deepest fear of incompetence and failure. Since we’ve established there is no proof that the other cards were wrong, let’s try to gently separate the *feeling* of uncertainty from the *reality* of the situation. When you imagine the worst-case scenario—that every previous card had a mistake you missed—do you think that specific image helps you solve the problem or makes it feel larger?

It definitely makes it feel larger. When I picture all those cards piling up with errors I didn't catch, I just feel so hopeless and small. Like nothing I do is good enough. It doesn't help me fix anything — it just makes me want to stop proofreading altogether.

That sense of hopelessness is heartbreaking to hear, and it makes complete sense that imagining a mountain of undetected errors would make you feel small and lead you to quit. It sounds like your brain is interpreting the *possibility* of future mistakes as proof that your current efforts were worthless. To help clarify this, if we look strictly at the evidence we gathered yesterday—you caught errors successfully and your boss treats mistakes as normal—does seeing those facts alongside the "mountain of errors" image suggest that the disaster you're fearing is actually happening right now, or is it just a story playing out in your head?

Looking at it that way... I guess it's more of a story. I mean, my boss did say it was okay and that these things happen. And I have caught plenty of mistakes over the months I've been there. It's just so hard not to feel like one slip-up means I'm failing at everything.

You are absolutely right to spot that disconnect; your boss's words and your track record of catching errors form a solid foundation, while the feeling of total failure is a story your brain is telling itself. It seems like the core struggle isn't just about the specific cards, but the belief that one slip-up erases all your past successes and makes you incapable. Before we settle on a concrete strategy, does the idea that "one slip-up doesn't erase your competence" resonate with you, or does it still feel like a dangerous assumption?

It does resonate... a little. I want to believe it, but there's this voice that says "but what if this time it's different" or "what if you're just fooling yourself." It feels risky to let go of that vigilance, like if I stop worrying so much, I'll get careless and miss even more mistakes.

That is a very common and understandable safety behavior; your brain believes that lowering its guard increases the risk of catastrophe, so it keeps the alarm system running at full volume. We could try a different approach instead of forcing you to ignore the warnings: what if we treated your vigilance as a necessary tool for *now*, but practiced gently challenging the "never wrong" story attached to it? Specifically, when that voice says "this time it will be different," could you try noting down one piece of past evidence where you handled a similar situation calmly and correctly?

I think I could try that. Like yesterday, I caught a spelling error in a birthday card before it went to print. I handled it fine, nobody got mad, and the card got fixed. So I guess that's evidence that I'm not just messing up all the time. Maybe writing those moments down could help quiet that voice, at least a little.

That is a brilliant realization; connecting yesterday's successful correction directly to the present worry creates a powerful link between your actions and your safety. By documenting that specific instance where you caught an error and everything turned out well, you provide your brain with a tangible fact that contradicts the "everything is falling apart" narrative. Would you be willing to commit to writing down one moment like that every day for the next few days, not to prove you are perfect, but simply to remind yourself that mistakes are rare and manageable?

I think I can commit to that. Just one small win each day, written down to look back on. It sounds manageable, not like I have to fix everything at once. Thank you, that feels... a bit lighter already.

That is a wonderful perspective shift; framing it as collecting "small wins" rather than fixing everything removes the overwhelming pressure and makes the task feel truly achievable. You are building a personal archive of evidence that shows you are capable and resilient, which serves as a reliable antidote to the scary stories in your head. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure you feel confident in this plan: does the idea of jotting down one daily example of handling a mistake comfortably feel like the right next step for you, or would you prefer a slightly different way to track these moments?

No, I think this feels like the right step. One small thing a day is something I can actually do without getting overwhelmed. I'll start tonight with yesterday's spelling catch, and see how it goes from there. I feel like I'm not just spiraling anymore, and that's a good place to start.

That is a fantastic commitment; shifting from spiraling to actively recording evidence is a huge step forward in regaining control. Starting tonight with yesterday's success sets a perfect tone for the habit, proving to yourself that even one documented win is worth the effort. I am going to send you a gentle reminder tomorrow morning to check in on your notes and celebrate that first small win. Is there anything else you would like to discuss before we close our session today?

No, I think that covers everything for today. I feel more settled than when I walked in, which is really nice. Thank you for helping me see this differently. I'll work on that list and see you next time.

You are very welcome; it sounds like we made meaningful progress today by grounding your worries in real examples of your capability. Remember that simply writing down one small win is a victory in itself, and I will reach out tomorrow to encourage you about your first entry. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how your daily notes go next time.
