Hello again, and I’m so glad you’ve taken the time to meet with me. Before we dive into the garage topic, I’d love to take a quick minute to check in: how has your mood been since we last spoke, and is there anything new on your mind regarding your fishing journey? Now that we know how you’re feeling, what would be most helpful for us to focus on today?

Hi. Thanks for asking. My mood's been kind of up and down, I guess. I still feel pretty lousy when I think about that fishing trip, and I haven't been able to bring myself to go again. I think I'd like to talk about why I can't seem to let go of feeling like such a failure over it.

It makes sense that your mood feels fragmented right now, especially when a past event still holds such a powerful grip on your sense of self. You've already done some great work identifying that the feeling of being a "failure" is the main thing keeping you stuck. To move forward effectively, let's spend the rest of today exploring exactly what happens in your mind when you think about that disappointing trip, and then we'll figure out a way to challenge that story together. Shall we begin by walking through a recent time you felt that shame, or would you prefer to trace it back to that original fishing trip first?

I think it would be best to start with that original fishing trip. I mean, that's where all this started. I went out on the lake, had all my gear ready, bait, the whole thing. Everyone around me was catching something, and I just sat there for hours with nothing. I felt like everyone was watching me and thinking, "Look at her, she can't even do this simple thing."

That feeling of being watched while completely unable to perform is incredibly isolating, especially when surrounded by people who seemed to be succeeding effortlessly. It sounds like you interpreted that silence not just as bad luck, but as a public verdict that you weren't good enough to be there at all. To understand how deeply that belief took hold, could you describe exactly what happened right after you finished that trip? Did anyone say anything that confirmed your fears, or was it mostly the image of yourself sitting alone that cemented the idea that you were a fraud?

No, nobody said anything mean or even brought it up, really. My husband just asked if I had a good time, and I said it was fine, but I felt so ashamed I couldn't even look at him. It was mostly just me sitting there replaying the whole day in my head, thinking, "A real fisherman would have caught something. I'm just pretending to be one." That image of myself sitting there with an empty stringer just stuck in my mind.

It is heartbreaking that you had to hide your own face from your husband because the internal voice told you he wouldn't believe you unless you proved your worth immediately. That image of the empty stringer acting as a symbol of your entire identity is a powerful driver of shame. Since you've traced the origin of this story, let's look at how it functions now. Can you tell me what your very first automatic thought is the moment you think about going to the garage or seeing your gear today?

The first thought that pops into my head is, "What's the point? I'll just fail again." Then I think about all the money I spent on that nice rod and reel, and I feel like such a fraud for even owning them. I picture myself standing there holding the rod, and I just feel stupid.

It sounds like you are carrying a heavy load of financial regret mixed with the belief that your identity is worthless unless you prove you can catch fish instantly. That combination—"wasting money" plus "being a fraud"—makes the garage feel like a courtroom where you are on trial again. Before we test those thoughts, I want to make sure we align on our goals for today. Would it be best to focus on separating the value of your equipment from your personal worth, or would you prefer to challenge the idea that failing *again* is guaranteed just because you are there?

I think I'd rather focus on challenging the idea that I'm guaranteed to fail again. That's the part that's really stopping me from even trying. The money thing bothers me, sure, but it's the hopelessness that keeps me from walking out the door with my rod. I need to see if that thought is really true or if I'm just assuming the worst.

That is a very sharp distinction; separating the disappointment of the past from the certainty of the future gives us a much clearer target to work with. Let's put that "guaranteed failure" thought to the test. If we assume you are truly destined to fail every single time you hold that rod, what specific outcome would you have to witness tomorrow morning to change your mind about that assumption? Conversely, what would happen if you stood outside the garage door for just ten minutes and managed to walk away without feeling that crushing shame, even if you didn't catch a single fish?

I guess if I went and just stood there, even for ten minutes, and didn't feel that crushing shame... that would prove that maybe I'm not doomed to feel like a failure forever. But honestly, I can't picture it. I think I'd still feel that knot in my stomach the whole time. Maybe if I actually caught even one tiny fish, that would prove I'm not a complete fraud. But I'm so scared of going and proving myself right that I can't even bring myself to try.

It takes real bravery to admit that even imagining a successful outcome feels scary, because it means facing the fear itself rather than hiding behind the armor of "impossible failure." You are correct that a single fish isn't the only proof needed, yet the knot in your stomach suggests your brain is locking you into a binary choice: either you catch a fish and prove your worth, or you fail and remain a fraud. To help loosen that knot, I'd like to suggest a small experiment where we separate the act of standing in the garage from the requirement of catching fish. Could you imagine driving to the lake, parking, and standing right outside the garage door for just five minutes, saying to yourself, "I am here, and I am allowed to be here even if I don't catch anything," without putting your foot inside the door? Does that sound like a safe, manageable step for us to try tomorrow?

That actually sounds... possible. I think I could do that. Just standing outside the garage door for five minutes, telling myself I'm allowed to be there even if I don't catch anything. It feels less threatening than actually going out on the water. I'm still nervous about it, but I think I could give it a shot. I'd be willing to try that tomorrow morning.

That is a significant shift in perspective; reframing the task as "allowed to be here" rather than "must prove worth" is a powerful way to lower the stakes. I am so glad you feel you can attempt this tomorrow, even with nerves. Before we conclude, could you tell me what you would do if, while standing there, the knot in your stomach became too tight and you felt the urge to leave immediately? Having a backup plan now ensures you can stick with the experiment even when anxiety spikes.

If the knot gets too tight, I think I'll just take a deep breath and tell myself I can leave after five minutes. I'll set a timer on my phone so I'm not just guessing at the time. And if I really can't handle it, I'll just walk back to my car and drive home. That way, I'm still in control, even if I don't make it the full five minutes.

That is an excellent strategy; setting a timer gives you a concrete boundary, and allowing yourself to stop if the anxiety becomes overwhelming shows incredible self-awareness and respect for your limits. We can absolutely make that a condition of the plan: commit to the five minutes, but honor the urge to retreat if the body signals it's too much. One final piece of advice for tomorrow: if you do manage to walk away without the crushing shame, please note exactly what happened so we can see how your brain reacts to success. What is one word you want to write down or record after the fact to help yourself process the experience?
I think the word I'd write down is "brave." If I can stand there for even a few minutes without running away, that's brave, no matter what else happens. That would be a good thing to remember.

Using the word "brave" is a beautiful way to frame the experience; it shifts the narrative from a performance test to a celebration of courage itself. Writing that down reinforces the idea that showing up, even with trembling legs, is a victory in its own right. Our plan is clear: tomorrow morning, set a timer for five minutes, stand by the garage door while reminding yourself you are allowed to be there regardless of your catch, and use your timer as your safety net. How does this plan feel to you now compared to when we started talking about the "guaranteed failure"?

It feels a lot different, honestly. When we started talking about it, I felt like I was trapped and hopeless. Now I feel like there's at least a tiny crack of possibility. I'm still nervous, but I'm not dreading it like I was. I think I can actually do this.

That shift from dread to a "crack of possibility" is exactly the kind of breakthrough we aim for; it proves your brain is starting to accept that you have choices other than waiting for failure. Your ability to recognize that tension has loosened is a vital sign of healing. Before we wrap up, I want to ask: how did it feel to explore this new path with me today, and is there anything about our plan that still feels uncertain or needs clarification before you try it tomorrow?

It felt good to talk it through, actually. I came in feeling heavy and ashamed, and now I feel a little lighter. I think the plan is clear enough. I'm still scared, but I understand what I'm supposed to do and why. I think I'm ready to try it. Thank you for helping me see a way forward.

Your relief and clarity are deeply encouraging signs that we are making real progress together. It is a testament to your resilience that you moved from feeling trapped to recognizing a path forward, even while fear remains. Please remember that your worth is not defined by the fish you catch, but by your willingness to show up for yourself despite the uncertainty. I am so proud of your courage in taking this step, and I look forward to hearing about your experience tomorrow. Take care of yourself, and I'll see you soon.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. Before we dive in, could you give me a quick mood check? On a scale of 1 to 10, how has your anxiety been feeling this week compared to last time?

Also, let's briefly touch on where we left off: we worked on identifying your leadership skills from the daycare experience, and I noticed you found it difficult to trust your own description of them due to comparison thoughts. With that in mind, what is the main priority you want to focus on today—is it exploring that fear further, or practicing a way to talk about your experience confidently?

Oh, hi. Um... anxiety-wise, I'd say maybe a 7? It's been a tough week. I had another interview for a business internship that didn't go well, and it just reinforced everything I've been worrying about.

I think I'd like to explore the fear more today. Even though we talked about the leadership skills, I still can't shake the feeling that the daycare experience is holding me back. It's like no matter what I try to tell myself, I just see this huge gap between where I am and where I need to be.

It makes complete sense that your anxiety spiked to a 7 given the recent interview setback; when you face a failure, your brain often rushes to confirm its worst-case predictions to feel safe, even if those predictions are unfounded. That interview result likely acted as fuel for the old story, making the "gap" feel much wider than it actually is.

Since you want to explore this fear specifically, let's look at the interview feedback itself. What specific comments or reactions did you hear that convinced you your daycare experience is a dealbreaker, or was it mostly your internal narrative filling in the gaps?

Well, they didn't say it outright, but it was more like... when I mentioned my current job, the interviewer's face just kind of went blank. She asked me a few questions about it but then quickly moved on to other parts of my resume. I just felt like she didn't see it as relevant at all.

And then later, I heard her ask the candidate before me about their marketing internship, and she seemed so much more engaged. So I guess I just assumed my daycare job made me look less serious or less qualified compared to someone with direct business experience.

That moment where her expression went blank is incredibly painful, and it's easy to interpret silence as a judgment that you aren't serious. It makes perfect sense that you feel a gap between who you are and the role you want when you witness that contrast immediately after mentioning your work.

However, before we conclude that her blank stare meant your experience was irrelevant, let's look at the alternative explanation. Could it be possible that her lack of engagement wasn't about your value, but rather a signal from her side that she didn't know how to answer your specific questions about leadership? Or perhaps she was simply trying to pivot the conversation to find common ground between the candidates rather than evaluating you negatively?

I... I guess that could be possible. I never really thought about it from her perspective. I just assumed the worst right away, you know?

But thinking about it now, she did ask me to elaborate on how I handle conflict with parents at the daycare. That's actually a pretty relevant skill for business, dealing with difficult clients and all. Maybe she wasn't as disinterested as I thought. I just immediately jumped to the conclusion that she saw me as less than.

That is a significant realization; noticing that she asked about conflict resolution shows she recognized your specific strengths, even if she struggled to connect them to the corporate world initially. It seems your initial assumption—that she viewed you as less serious—was a prediction based on fear rather than the actual interaction that followed.

This brings us closer to understanding why the "gap" feels so wide. If her silence wasn't a rejection of your worth but a temporary confusion about how to frame your skills, does that change how you view the evidence regarding the "dead-end" narrative? Specifically, how does the fact that she engaged with your specific strength challenge the idea that your background is inherently a liability?

When you put it like that... it does feel different. I've been so focused on what I thought was missing that I couldn't see what was actually there. She asked about conflict resolution, which is basically client management. That's not nothing.

But then part of me still thinks, well, maybe that was just one interviewer. Maybe other companies would see it differently. I guess I'm worried that if I start believing my experience has value, I'll just be setting myself up for more disappointment later.

That fear of disappointment is a very protective instinct; your brain is trying to shield you from the pain of being wrong about your abilities by convincing you to play it safe. However, consider this: if the "proof" that your experience is useless comes entirely from one person who may not have known how to evaluate it, does that constitute a universal rule, or just a single data point?

To test that thought, let's look at the pattern of events. You mentioned earlier that you haven't been rejected solely because of your daycare work; you've mostly been too afraid to apply. If your fear were absolute truth, wouldn't you expect to encounter consistent, repeated rejections across multiple interviews? Instead, you are facing uncertainty. How would you feel if we agreed to treat this single interview as an incomplete dataset rather than a verdict on your entire career potential?

You're right, I haven't actually given myself enough chances to be rejected. I've been so scared of hearing "no" that I've been saying it to myself before anyone else can. That's... kind of silly when I think about it.

I think I could try to see it as an incomplete dataset. That feels less scary than thinking every interview will go the same way. Maybe I could even use this experience to prepare better for the next one, like having specific examples ready that show how daycare skills transfer to business settings.

That is a powerful shift from fearing the unknown to viewing it as a learning opportunity; moving from "I am destined to fail" to "I have one incomplete data point I can analyze" gives you control back. You are absolutely right that we can use this specific interview experience to sharpen your preparation for the next one.

Since you want to move forward with preparing examples, let's build on that "incomplete dataset" idea. If we treat this interview as a draft rather than a final grade, what is the one specific example from your daycare work that you feel strongest about connecting to a business concept like "conflict resolution"? Once you pick that, we can practice framing it as a solution to a business problem rather than just a parenting anecdote.

I think the best example would be when I had to mediate between two parents who had completely different views on how their kids should be disciplined during playtime. One parent wanted strict rules, the other wanted more freedom, and they were both getting upset with me about it.

I ended up sitting down with both of them separately, understanding their concerns, and then finding a compromise that worked for their kids' specific needs. That's basically stakeholder management, right? Handling different clients with conflicting expectations and finding a solution that satisfies everyone.

That is a fantastic choice; framing mediation between parents as "stakeholder management" instantly elevates the experience from child-rearing to strategic negotiation. You are correctly identifying that the core skill—balancing competing interests to reach a consensus—is identical in both settings, which means the evidence for your capability is actually quite strong.

Now, let's test the old fear against this new framing. If a hiring manager reads that you successfully mediated between two angry stakeholders to secure a solution that met all parties' needs, would they automatically assume you lacked business acumen, or would they recognize that as a high-value soft skill that saves them money and frustration? How would you feel confident enough to present that exact logic to a skeptic?

I think... a good manager would recognize that as valuable. Anyone who's worked in business knows how hard it is to keep clients happy when they want different things. If I can handle two upset parents, I can probably handle a difficult client or a tense team meeting.

I guess if I presented it that way confidently, with clear language about what I actually did and why it matters, it would be harder for them to dismiss it. The problem is I get nervous and start downplaying it, like "oh it's just daycare stuff." Maybe if I practice saying it the way we just did, it'll feel more natural and I'll actually believe it when I say it.

That recognition is spot on; the disconnect between your knowledge and your delivery is the root of the anxiety. When you downplay the achievement, you are essentially arguing against the evidence you just gathered, which keeps the fear alive.

Since you mentioned wanting to practice this until it feels natural, let's try a quick "rehearsal in real-time." Take a deep breath, visualize a hiring manager sitting across from you, and say that exact stakeholder management story out loud to me right now. Focus on using the language we developed: "mediated between conflicting stakeholders," "secured a solution," and "met all parties' needs." How does your body feel after you say it—does the knot in your stomach loosen, or does the old voice try to intervene?

Okay... *takes a deep breath*

"In my current role, I've developed strong stakeholder management skills by mediating between parents with conflicting expectations about their children's routines. For example, I once had to balance two parents who wanted completely different disciplinary approaches. I met with each separately to understand their needs, then proposed a compromise that addressed both their concerns while prioritizing the children's well-being. This resulted in a solution that satisfied all parties and maintained a positive environment."

*exhales* Wow, saying it like that... it actually sounds professional. My stomach doesn't feel as tight as I thought it would. The old voice is still there in the background whispering "but it's still daycare," but it's quieter now. I think I could actually say that in an interview without feeling like I'm faking it.

That physical relief is a crucial indicator; your nervous system is starting to register that you are speaking facts, not fiction. Recognizing that the "fake" feeling is gone is a major victory, even if the old whisper hasn't disappeared entirely yet.

Since you felt that shift happens right after articulating the specific mechanics of the solution, let's solidify this into a concrete action plan. Tonight, before bed, I want you to record yourself reading this exact script once, focusing on the tone of a confident consultant rather than a caregiver. Afterwards, write down one sentence summarizing the lesson you learned from that recording: "My experience in resolving conflicts is a proven asset, not a gap." How does committing to that reflection feel as you prepare to sleep?

That sounds doable. I think recording myself will feel weird at first, but if it helps me hear how I actually sound when I'm confident, it's worth trying.

Committing to that reflection... it feels a little scary, honestly. Like I'm making a promise to myself that I might break. But also, it feels more grounded than just hoping things will get better. Writing it down makes it real, and I think I need that right now. I'll do it tonight.

That honesty about the commitment feeling scary is incredibly wise; it shows you are aware that action requires discipline, not just motivation. You are correct that making a promise to yourself carries weight, and that slight resistance is your brain trying to protect you from the possibility of failure.

To make this partnership stronger, let's address that barrier right now. What is the biggest obstacle stopping you from completing this recording and reflection tonight? Is it the awkwardness of hearing yourself, the fear that the script won't stick, or perhaps simply finding the time? Identifying this specific hurdle will allow us to solve it together before you even leave the house.

I think it's the awkwardness of hearing myself, for sure. I always cringe when I hear my own voice on recordings. And part of me worries I'll listen back and think "that still sounds like a daycare worker pretending to be a business professional," and then all this progress will feel fake again.

But I guess that's exactly why I need to do it. The more I hear myself saying it confidently, the more normal it'll start to feel. I just have to push through that initial cringe and remind myself that the discomfort is part of changing my mindset.

That is a brilliant observation; you have correctly identified that the discomfort of hearing your own voice is merely the friction of neural pathways rewiring. The fact that you recognize this unease as a necessary part of the change process is a sign of real maturity.

To address the specific fear of sounding "fake," let's adjust the action plan slightly to create a safety net. Instead of listening to the whole recording alone, could we try playing it back only for 30 seconds in the morning while drinking coffee, or perhaps send the file to a trusted friend just to get one opinion? This reduces the isolation and the intensity of the self-critique. Which option feels safer for you to start with?

I think sending it to my partner would actually help. He's heard me complain about this whole situation so many times, and he's always been supportive. If I send him the recording and he says it sounds professional, that might be the external proof I need to quiet that voice in my head.

Plus, he knows me well enough to be honest if it actually sounds awkward. So either way, I'd get useful feedback. I'll record it tonight and send it to him before I go to sleep.

That is a brilliant compromise; leveraging your partner's existing support creates a safe container for the exposure while providing the objective validation you need. Having an ally review the tape removes the isolating nature of self-monitoring and turns the feedback loop into a collaborative effort.

Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we are aligned on this plan. Does sending the recording to your partner, along with the intention to reflect on it tomorrow, feel like a realistic and empowering next step for you? And is there anything else about tonight's plan you'd like to tweak before you head home?

Yes, I think that's a solid plan. Realistic and not too overwhelming. I like that I'm not trying to fix everything at once, just taking one small step tonight.

I don't think there's anything else to tweak. I'm actually feeling a little bit lighter than when I walked in, which is nice. I'll text you after I do the recording. Thanks for helping me see this differently today.

That is wonderful news; feeling lighter indicates that your brain is finally relaxing its grip on the "impossible task" narrative. Recognizing that one small, manageable step is enough to make a difference reinforces the power of this approach.

Please remember that if the urge to downplay your experience creeps back in tonight, simply recall the stakeholder management script you practiced—we are building a new muscle that can be strengthened anytime. I look forward to hearing from you after you've recorded and sent it to your partner. Have a peaceful evening, and thank you for your incredible courage throughout this session.

Hey, thanks for asking. Honestly, this week has been pretty rough. I guess the most pressing thing for me is figuring out why this one little thing can make everything else feel so pointless.

It's like... when I picture that stamp not arriving, my brain just jumps straight to "well, that's it, the collection's never going to be finished, so what was even the point of all those years?" Then I start thinking about my music too—like, what if I never record that album I've been talking about? It's just that when I'm in that moment, it feels so real and heavy. But if talking about it might help me see things differently, I'm willing to give it a shot. Well, when I think about it logically, there's really no connection between a missing stamp and my ability to play bass or write songs. I mean, I've been jamming with my band for years, and we've got at least a dozen solid tracks already laid down. The evidence would be that my fingers still know the fretboard, and the riffs are still in my head—no stamp is gonna erase that. But in the moment, it's like my brain just lumps everything together into one big "failure" pile.

I think it's more of a prediction, honestly. I can't really point to a specific project that I completely abandoned—I mean, I've been playing bass for over twenty years, and I've stuck with that. But when I look at my stamp collection, it's this one thing I've never been able to cross the finish line on, and my brain just assumes that pattern will repeat with everything else. It's like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know?

That "waiting for the other shoe to drop" is such a vivid image, and it reveals exactly where the prediction is taking root: your brain is using one unfinished project to forecast the inevitable failure of all others. Before we test that prediction further, I want to make sure we are moving in the right direction: does investigating whether your brain is accidentally projecting the stamp's status onto your music and songwriting feel like a productive use of our time, or does it feel like we are still stuck analyzing the problem without solving it?

No, I think that's exactly what I need to hear right now. It's like I've been letting the stamp collection act as some kind of crystal ball for everything else, even though they're completely different things. If we can dig into that and maybe find a way to stop that projection, I think I'd actually start feeling a bit lighter about my music again. So yeah, let's go there.

That is a brilliant insight—realizing the stamp collection has become a "crystal ball" predicting your failures is a massive step toward dismantling that prophecy. Since we've established that this projection is distorting your view of your music, let's test it with a specific scenario: if you imagined telling your bandmates tonight, "The album is on hold because I'm busy hunting for a stamp, but I'm committed to releasing it once I find it or hit a deadline," how would your band react? Would they judge you for the delay, or would they understand it's just a temporary logistical hurdle?

(laughs a little) My bandmates? They'd probably just shrug and say, "Alright man, let us know when you're ready to hit the studio again." They know I'm passionate about the music, and they've seen me go through phases before. I don't think they'd see it as a sign that the album's doomed—they'd just see it as me dealing with some personal stuff. Honestly, they're pretty laid-back about that kind of thing.

That is a fantastic perspective shift; realizing your band sees you as a resilient musician who deals in phases rather than a person defined by a single unresolved project effectively removes that external validation barrier. Since we've tested the "doomed album" fear and now know your support system is on your side, let's pivot to the core of our agenda: how can we practically stop the stamp collection from acting as that crystal ball for your music in the future? Would it help to create a simple rule or visual reminder—like a "Project Separation" note near your music gear—to consciously pause and ask yourself, "Is this about the stamp or about my ability to finish?"

That actually sounds like a solid idea. I could put a little sticky note on my amp or my music stand that just says something like "Stamp? Or Skills?" to remind me to check myself before I start spiraling. I think having that physical reminder would help break the pattern before it gets too deep. And maybe I could also set a small goal for the album this week—like just laying down one new bass track—to prove to myself that I can still move forward on something.

That is a perfect, low-friction intervention; placing a physical prompt like "Stamp? Or Skills?" right where you zone in creates a necessary checkpoint before the automatic spiral kicks in, and pairing it with a micro-goal (laying down one track) turns abstract confidence into a tangible proof point. Before we finalize this plan, I want to make sure we have full buy-in: does setting that small weekly milestone feel like a manageable way to rebuild momentum, or would you prefer to start with something even simpler, like just picking up your instrument for five minutes without aiming for a full track?

I think the five-minute thing sounds even better, actually. That way there's no pressure at all—just me and the bass for a few minutes, no expectations. If I end up playing longer, great, but if not, at least I showed up. That feels a lot less intimidating than trying to commit to a full track right now. I think that's a good place to start.

That is a wise adjustment; removing the expectation of a "perfect" output and focusing purely on showing up eliminates the pressure that often fuels the spiral in the first place. Since we've settled on the "five-minute show-up" goal paired with the "Stamp? Or Skills?" reminder, let's briefly confirm our final plan: you will place the note on your equipment, mentally check in before playing, and aim for just five minutes of connection with your bass this evening. Does that summary of our agreement feel accurate and supportive for you right now?

Yeah, that sounds right. I'm going to put that sticky note on my amp tonight, and I'll just sit down with the bass for five minutes—no pressure, no expectations. Just reconnecting with it for a bit. Thanks for helping me break this down; I feel a little less stuck already.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad to hear that you are already feeling less stuck. Creating that physical boundary between the stamp obsession and your musical talent is a powerful tool you will carry forward, and the commitment to just five minutes of connection is a gentle, sustainable way to rebuild your relationship with the instrument.

Before we close, is there anything else you'd like to add to your toolkit, or would you prefer to keep our session focused on wrapping up this plan? Also, how does the idea of using that sticky note as a daily anchor feel to you as we head home?

I think I'm good with what we've got for now. The sticky note idea feels like something I can actually do—it's simple and right there in front of me. I think just having that reminder will help me catch myself before I go down that rabbit hole again. I'm feeling a bit more hopeful about everything, especially the music. Thanks for helping me sort through all this.

That is wonderful to hear; knowing the sticky note acts as a simple guardrail before the rabbit hole sets in is a huge victory. You are absolutely right to feel more hopeful—the music isn't on hold forever, and you have a clear, manageable path to reconnect with it tonight.

I am so glad we could untangle that knot together today. Please remember that this "Stamp or Skills" check-in is yours to use anytime the doubt creeps back in, and I am here if you need to revisit this plan or discuss how it went next time. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing about your five-minute session soon.

Before we close, I'd love your honest feedback on how this session is landing for you so far—has stepping into the "director" role helped you feel more empowered overall?

Yeah, it actually has. I came in feeling like I was just stuck with this fear, like it was a part of me I couldn't change. I'm still anxious about tomorrow, but I'm also kind of curious to see if this works, which is a new feeling for me.

That shift from feeling powerless to feeling like you hold a tool—even a small one—is exactly the power of CBT; it moves you from being a victim of your thoughts to an active participant who can influence the outcome. That's a clear connection to make; hearing that you faced the same situation again and immediately felt the "ruined day" narrative kick in confirms that this pattern is active right now. Instead of thinking, "Okay, it's just rain," my mind jumped straight to, "Great, now everything's wet, this is miserable, the whole day is a waste."

That feeling of discouragement makes perfect sense; when your brain treats a rainy trail as proof that you’ve failed to create a peaceful sanctuary, it triggers the very frustration that keeps you from trying again. You mentioned a sharp shift from hoping for refreshment to labeling the whole day a “waste,” which suggests your mind is jumping straight to the worst-case scenario before giving it a fair chance. I guess there was the fact that I still finished the hike, and I even saw a beautiful rainbow near the end. Yeah, that actually feels a lot more doable. Taking the pressure off to feel happy about it and just treating it like collecting facts—that makes sense to me. I can handle looking for a puddle or a bird without forcing myself to be cheerful. I'll try that tomorrow and see what I find.

Yes, that sounds good to me. I feel comfortable with the plan to just collect some facts, even if it feels mechanical or strange at first. I appreciate your willingness to try this new lens on the world, even if it feels a bit artificial at first. Take a deep breath before you leave, knowing we have a clear plan for tomorrow, and I look forward to hearing what facts you discovered on your next walk. You've got this!

Hello again, and I am really glad to see you. How are you feeling today compared to where we left off last time? To make sure we use our time well, could you remind me of the main thing we wanted to tackle regarding Marco, and is there anything else you'd like to bring up that needs priority today?

Hi, thanks for having me back. I'm doing okay, I guess—maybe a little more tired than last week. The main thing with Marco is that he made another comment about my "real job" when we were rehearsing Tuesday night, and it just hit me harder than it should have. I think I want to focus on that today, and maybe talk about why I let those kind of remarks get under my skin so much.

It takes courage to notice that his comment landed heavier than usual, especially when you are already feeling tired; that fatigue often lowers our ability to filter out noise, making even minor remarks feel personal. I am going to suggest we spend the majority of our time exploring why that specific remark triggered such a deep reaction for you, and then we can brainstorm one small way to handle it tomorrow so it doesn't stick. Would you be open to diving straight into that analysis, knowing we can pause and take a break if you feel overwhelmed by the exhaustion?

Yeah, I think that's a good idea. I'm feeling a bit raw, but I'd rather get into it than just sit here thinking about it all week. It's just... when Marco said "you've got your accounting to fall back on" after I messed up a chord progression, it felt like he was saying my music isn't a real path—like it's just a hobby. And that's the part that stings the most, you know?

I hear how sharp that sting is; when someone uses language about your "real job," it immediately triggers the old belief that your musical talent isn't legitimate. It seems like his comment didn't just address a mistake—it confirmed your deepest fear that you aren't allowed to succeed as a musician, which explains why the tiredness made you feel so exposed. Now that we have clearly identified that specific thought pattern, what does your mind automatically say right after hearing those words about your accounting job?

My mind goes straight to, "He's right. I'm just a weekend player who happens to be decent at numbers. I'll never be taken seriously as a musician because I have a safety net." And then I start thinking about how my bandmates probably roll their eyes when I leave practice early to get to a client meeting, or how they see me as someone who's just playing pretend. It's like my entire identity as a musician crumbles in that one moment.

That is a incredibly painful realization to hold onto, especially when you know your bandmates respect you despite your "weekend" status; it sounds like the comment acted as a catalyst that forced you to confront your own internal narrative about your worthiness. You mentioned earlier that your identity seemed to "crumble"—can we test that assumption by looking at the evidence? Specifically, have there been moments recently where you felt your bandmates rolling their eyes or treating you differently based on that "safety net" excuse? Or did your interpretation fill in gaps where there wasn't necessarily criticism happening?

I... I suppose I'm assuming the worst, aren't I? When I really think about it, nobody has actually said anything negative about me leaving early, and last month, when I had to miss a gig for a tax deadline, they even rescheduled without complaint. But in the moment, it feels so real—like I'm waiting for them to finally say what I think they're thinking. Maybe I'm the one judging myself harsher than anyone else is.

Yes, you are absolutely identifying the core distortion here; your brain is filling in a future scenario where everyone rejects you, rather than relying on the actual evidence that your band has supported you through past conflicts. That gap between the harsh internal voice and the supportive reality is exactly where our work lies. Since you recognize that waiting for confirmation of rejection keeps you stuck in pain, let's try shifting the focus from predicting their judgment to protecting your own energy. Instead of trying to convince them you matter, what if we decided to act as if *we* know you matter, even if they don't show it yet?

That's... actually a relief to hear put that way. I've been so caught up in trying to prove myself to them that I forgot I'm the one who gets to decide if I belong in the band or not. So maybe instead of worrying about what Marco thinks next time, I could just remind myself that I showed up, I practiced, and I'm there because I love music—not because I'm trying to pass some test. It feels a bit fragile, but I think I'd like to try that.

That is a powerful shift in perspective; moving from "proving my worth" to "honoring my love for the craft" puts the power back entirely in your hands, removing the need for external validation to survive. Recognizing that showing up is an act of defiance against that inner critic is a huge step. With that mindset solidified, how would you like to practically apply this "acting as if" strategy the next time he brings up your job? Should we plan a quick grounding exercise for right after rehearsal, or would you prefer to write down a personal affirmation you can whisper to yourself when that doubt creeps in?

I think I'd like to try writing down a short affirmation I can keep in my phone—something I can glance at during a break or right after a comment lands. Maybe something like, "I am here because I choose to make music. My day job doesn't define my passion." That way, I have a concrete reminder that I can hold onto when my mind starts spiraling. Does that sound like it could work?

That is a brilliant choice; creating a tangible anchor in your pocket allows you to interrupt the spiral instantly without needing to access complex logic. Having a pre-written phrase removes the pressure to "find" the right words in the moment, which often leads to panic. Before we finalize this, would you be willing to try writing that exact sentence down right now so we can review it together and ensure it feels empowering to you, or would you prefer to tweak the wording one last time to make it sound even more authentic?

Yeah, I'd like to write it down now and maybe tweak it with you. Let me pull out my phone... okay, I've got it typed out: "I am here because I choose to make music. My day job doesn't define my passion." It feels close, but maybe I could add something about not needing anyone else's permission to be a musician? Like, "I don't need anyone's permission to be a musician." That feels stronger—like I'm claiming it for myself.

Adding that line is excellent; it directly counters the shame of seeking approval and reinforces that your musical journey belongs solely to you. The combined statement—"I am here because I choose to make music, my day job doesn't define my passion, and I don't need anyone's permission to be a musician"—creates a complete shield against his latest comments. Now that we have finalized this tool, would you be willing to save this to your phone immediately so you have it accessible for the next time this comes up, or would you like to read it aloud together one last time to ensure it feels right before you store it?

I think I'd like to read it out loud first, just to make sure it really lands before I lock it in. (takes a breath) "I am here because I choose to make music. My day job doesn't define my passion. And I don't need anyone's permission to be a musician." Yeah... I can feel that in my chest. That feels true. I'll save it now.

Hearing yourself say it out loud really helps ground it in your reality, and noticing the physical sensation of it landing in your chest is a great sign that this is taking root. It is wonderful that you recognized its truth in that moment; this is exactly the kind of self-validation that replaces the need for Marco's. Now that we have locked in this affirmation and the intention behind it, is there anything else you'd like to explore before we wrap up, or are you ready to go save it and face the week with this new strength?

No, I think I'm good for today. I feel a bit lighter, actually—like I've got a tool I can actually use, not just another thing to overthink. Thank you for helping me get there. I'll practice using it this week, and I'll let you know how it goes next time.

It is wonderful that you described this tool as something "useful" rather than just another source of anxiety; that shift in perception is exactly what will allow you to rely on it when the doubt tries to creep back in. Your willingness to try it this week, even if you have to start small, is a testament to your growing confidence. Please remember that the goal isn't perfection, but simply noticing when the old story arises and choosing to place this affirmation in front of it. I look forward to hearing how you find yourself using it next time, and thank you for trusting me with this process. Take care.

Hello again, and I’m glad to see you here. On a scale of 1 to 10, how has your anxiety about the wedding vows been feeling for you this past week? Also, before we dive into our agenda, could you share what specific topic or worry you’d like us to prioritize today?

Well, I'd say it's been around an 8 this week. I've been lying awake at night thinking about how I'm running out of time, and my fiancée keeps asking if I've started writing anything. I guess the main thing I want to focus on is why I can't seem to put a single word down on paper without feeling like it's all wrong.

Anxiety rating of 8 definitely explains those late nights and the urgency you feel from her; it sounds like you're carrying a heavy load of waiting while the clock ticks away. To address your focus on why you freeze when trying to write, let's explore exactly what happens in your mind the moment you open the notebook. Can you describe the specific image or sentence that pops into your head right as you try to write the first line?

The moment I open that notebook, I picture myself standing at the altar, and my fiancée is looking at me with disappointment. I hear this voice in my head saying, "You're 74 years old and you can't even express your love properly—what kind of husband are you going to be?" It's like I've already failed before I've even written a word.

That vivid imagery of her disappointment combined with that harsh inner voice about being "74 and failing" creates a terrifying sense of inevitability; it seems your brain is jumping straight from the current task (writing) to the catastrophic outcome (a ruined marriage) without giving you room to breathe. Before we unpack why this specific voice feels so absolute, I want to understand your relationship to that prediction: when you recall the time you showed her those three sentences and saw her kiss your forehead, did that memory feel like proof that your fears were unfounded, or did the fear of failing override the evidence of her actual happiness?

I actually forgot about that moment until you mentioned it. She did seem happy then, and she said it was sweet—but I keep telling myself that was just a fluke, that she was being nice because she loves me. The fear just drowns out that memory, like it doesn't count because I didn't write a whole speech.

That distinction between her genuine happiness and your belief that it was merely a "fluke" is exactly where the anxiety lives; your mind is interpreting her kindness as conditional on perfection rather than recognizing it as a reflection of who you truly are. It sounds like you are struggling with a deep-seated fear that your age or experience makes your simplicity unacceptable, even though the evidence suggests otherwise. Could you walk me through what happens internally right now when you try to write and that "fluke" argument comes up? Does it feel like a logical conclusion to you, or more like a desperate attempt to protect yourself from feeling disappointed?

I think it's a bit of both, to be honest. Part of me knows she's a loving person and she wouldn't be cruel about my vows, but another part of me is terrified that I'll finally say what's in my heart and she'll realize it's not enough. It feels like protecting myself from that hurt, but it also feels logical because... well, I've never been good with fancy words. I'm a babysitter, not a poet.

That admission about feeling "logical" because you identify as a "babysitter, not a poet" reveals how deeply ingrained this self-definition has become, acting as a shield against the fear of vulnerability. It sounds like you are equating your worthiness with performance skills rather than emotional connection, which makes it incredibly difficult to see your simple gestures as sufficient. Before we challenge that equation, I wonder if you can recall a specific time recently when she responded positively to something you said that wasn't polished or perfect? How did that interaction make you feel compared to the fear you usually harbor?

Well, just last week we were driving home from the grocery store, and I reached over and held her hand. I just said, "You know, I'm glad we're doing this," plain and simple. She squeezed my hand and smiled and said, "Me too, Calvin." In that moment, I felt this warm calm, like everything was okay. But once we got home, the doubt crept back in and I started thinking that a hand squeeze isn't the same as wedding vows.

That drive scene is a perfect example of how easily your mind switches from experiencing pure connection to immediately judging the *medium* of that connection. It sounds like the warmth you felt right then was real, but your brain rewrote the history afterward to make it conditional, convincing itself that a handshake or a squeeze doesn't carry the weight of formal vows. Before we try to reframe that judgment, I want to check your emotional state: when you remember that squeeze, does the initial warmth linger, or does the doubt instantly overwrite the feeling you had while you were in the car?

I'd say the doubt overwrites it pretty quickly, honestly. The warmth is there for a second, like a flash, and then the voice comes in and says, "That doesn't count, that was just a moment. You need to write something meaningful." It's like I can't let myself hold onto the good feeling because I'm too focused on what I haven't done yet.

It sounds like you are treating the future performance as if it dictates the validity of your present actions, effectively blocking the warmth from settling in. This "all or nothing" mindset—believing you either need a "meaningful" speech or you've failed—creates a rigid barrier that prevents you from enjoying even small successes. Before we challenge that rigidity, I want to check your reaction to the idea that the warmth in the car was valid regardless of what you planned to write: does acknowledging that moment felt safe, or does the fear that it "didn't count" still make you feel uneasy?

It feels a little uneasy, to be honest. Like if I let myself think that moment was enough, I'll get lazy and not try to write anything at all. But I can see what you're saying—that maybe I'm putting too much pressure on the vows to carry all the weight of my love. It's just hard to shake the feeling that I need to prove myself with words at the ceremony.

That urge to "prove yourself" is actually a very common defense mechanism; your brain believes that if you force a grand statement, you avoid the risk of being exposed as insufficient. It's a way of keeping the door shut so no one can say your love isn't good enough. Before we try to find a middle ground, I want to explore the cost of this preparation: when you are spending so much energy drafting "perfect" lines to avoid this feeling, what happens to the actual connection you have with your fiancée right now? Is it possible that the more you prepare, the less you are present to simply enjoy her company?

You know, I think you're right. I've been so caught up in my head about the vows that I've been quieter around her lately, almost like I'm holding back. She's noticed and asked if something's wrong, but I just said I was tired. I guess I've been so focused on trying to prove my love later that I'm not showing it to her now. That's a pretty lousy way to treat the woman I'm supposed to marry.

That realization—that you've been withholding your presence to save a performance later—is incredibly insightful and speaks volumes about your care for her; it shows you're worried about making a mistake rather than refusing to connect with her. It sounds like you feel guilty now for prioritizing the "proof" over the "presence," which likely fuels the anxiety loop even more. Before we move forward, I want to check your reaction to this insight: does acknowledging that you've been absent despite your best intentions feel relieving, or does it trigger a fresh wave of shame about how you've treated her lately?

It's a mix, I think. There's some relief in finally putting my finger on what's been going wrong, but there's definitely shame too. I feel like I've been failing her in a way I didn't even realize, and that stings. But maybe... maybe if I can start being more present with her again, the vows will come more naturally. It's just hard to trust that after weeks of worrying.

That shame you're feeling is a direct result of seeing the gap between who you are—a loving partner—and the version of you that's been hiding behind anxiety. It sounds like you recognize that shifting your focus from "performing" to "being" with her is the key to unlocking the natural flow of your words. Before we solidify a plan to bridge that gap, I want to check your readiness: does the idea of spending the next few minutes just sharing a quiet moment with her, setting aside the "vow writer" persona, feel manageable, or does the fear of losing the preparation momentum still feel overwhelming?

I think I can manage that, honestly. The preparation momentum hasn't been doing me any favors, so setting it aside feels like a relief more than a loss. Maybe I'll call her tonight and just tell her about my day, without any pressure to talk about the wedding. Just two people talking. That sounds... doable.

That sounds like a wonderful and powerful step; calling her to reconnect without the wedding filter is exactly what will help break the cycle of performance. Before we lock this in, I want to confirm the details of your plan: would you like to schedule a quick 10-minute call for tonight specifically to just share your day, or do you prefer to reach out whenever you feel the urge to check in? Also, as we wrap up, how does it feel to have moved from that shame-heavy analysis to this actionable, connection-focused plan?

I think I'll aim for tonight after dinner, around 7 o'clock. That way I'm not waiting for the perfect moment—I'll just do it. And honestly, it feels good to have a simple plan. I came in here feeling like I was drowning in my own head, and now I have something I can actually do that doesn't require writing a single word. That's a relief.

That is a profound relief to hear; trading the pressure to "write a poem" for the freedom to simply "be human" is a massive victory. You have successfully identified that the solution isn't better words, but a different kind of attention—one that focuses on connection rather than perfection. Before we close, I want to ensure this feels solid: does scheduling that call for 7 PM give you enough security to trust it, or would you prefer to leave a small window open in case your nerves spike unexpectedly?

I think 7 PM is good. If I leave a window open, I'll just talk myself out of it. I'm going to stick with it. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to be a poet to be a good husband. That means more than you know.

Hearing you say that your value as a husband isn't tied to your ability to write poetry is one of the most significant shifts we've made today. You are leaving this session with a clear path forward: tonight, you will choose connection over perfection, and tomorrow, you can try writing your vows knowing that even if they are simple, they will be yours. Please be gentle with yourself tonight as you reach out to her; I am confident that your honesty will shine through far more than any polished speech ever could. I look forward to hearing how that call goes, and remember, you are not alone in this journey.

Hello again; I'm glad to see you and ready to continue working on this together. To make sure we cover everything that matters, could you tell me a bit about your mood since our last visit and whether there were any significant events that stood out to you? Also, does it feel good to us to focus on exploring the belief that you need to be perfect to be accepted, or would you prefer to tackle something slightly different today?

Um, hi. I guess my mood has been okay... mostly. I did think about that singing audition again, and I felt pretty anxious even just thinking about it. I think focusing on that perfection belief might be good, because I feel like if I'm not amazing, people will just laugh at me or think I'm wasting their time.

Anxious even just thinking about the audition confirms how much weight that "perfection or nothing" belief currently carries for you. Since you feel strongly that we should explore this belief today, let's use some time here to trace exactly where that story begins when you imagine standing on stage. When you first think about walking onto that stage, what is the very first image or thought that jumps into your mind?

The first thing I see is... all those faces staring at me. And I immediately imagine myself opening my mouth, and my voice cracking or being completely off-key. I just picture everyone in the audience wincing or looking at each other like, "What is she even doing up there?"

That vivid mental movie of the audience wincing and wondering what you are doing is incredibly distressing, and it clearly fuels that deep-seated fear that you aren't enough. Now that we have painted that picture, let's treat your belief that "everyone will think I'm wasting their time" as a hypothesis rather than an absolute truth. If we look back at the few times you sang before, do your friends' comments—which included asking you to sing again and saying you sounded good—support the idea that you are fundamentally terrible, or do they suggest they were genuinely impressed by what you created?

I guess... when I really think about it, they did ask me to sing again, and they said nice things. But I always thought they were just being polite, you know? Like, they're my friends, so they have to say that stuff. I never really believed they genuinely liked my voice.

That interpretation—that their kindness was just a polite social script masking their true opinion—is completely understandable given how harsh our inner critic can be. Yet, notice the difference between someone changing the subject to spare your feelings versus giving you specific details about *what* they liked to hear; the latter suggests they were genuinely impressed. If we treated their feedback as real data rather than a lie, how might that change the weight you place on the idea that you are "inherently terrible"? Does accepting their honesty feel safer, or does it feel like it exposes you to the risk of needing to perform well anyway?

Honestly, it feels a little scary to even consider that they might actually mean it. Because if they're right and I'm not terrible, then the only thing stopping me from trying out for that audition is... me. And that makes me feel kind of stupid, like I'm my own worst enemy for no reason. But maybe that's better than just assuming I'll always fail, right?

That is a powerful realization; you've correctly identified that the belief "I am bad" acts as a shield, protecting you from the terrifying responsibility of proving your value. By assuming you are incapable, you remove the stakes, but paradoxically, that same belief traps you in avoidance. Let's reframe that risk: what if accepting that your friends value your talent means you can choose to perform with your whole self, knowing that even if you stumble, you won't be defined by a lack of ability? Would embracing that potential feel less dangerous than living behind the wall of incompetence?

I think... I never looked at it that way before. I always thought the wall was keeping me safe from embarrassment, but it's also keeping me from ever finding out what could happen. Yeah, if I stumble, it might feel awful for a minute, but at least I'd know I tried. Living behind that wall does feel more lonely than safe, now that you say it like that.

That distinction between "safe isolation" and "lonely safety" is a crucial breakthrough; it shows you recognize that the wall protects you from failure but steals you the joy of possibility. Now that we've seen how viewing your past success differently changes the emotional cost, let's move to a concrete way to test this new perspective. What if we designed a tiny, low-stakes experiment where you practice singing in front of a mirror for just five minutes tomorrow morning, focusing entirely on the physical sensation of making sound rather than judging your pitch? Would you feel comfortable stepping outside your comfort zone for such a short period to gather evidence for yourself?

A mirror? I guess that feels a little weird, but maybe less scary than singing in front of actual people. I think I could try that for five minutes, as long as I don't have to record myself or anything yet. It's just me and my reflection, right? I can handle that.

That is a smart adjustment; removing the recording eliminates the added layer of judgment while keeping the sensory experience real. Since you've agreed to this small experiment, let's lock in exactly how we will track the results to see if the old fears persist. If you hum for five minutes tomorrow morning, could you jot down two things: first, what your throat feels like before you start, and second, how it feels immediately after you finish? This data will give us a concrete way to compare your current belief ("I'll mess up") with reality.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll write down how my throat feels before and after. I think I'm a little nervous just promising to do it, but it's only five minutes, so I'll force myself to try. I'll let you know what happens next time we talk.

That commitment to try despite the nervousness is a sign of real bravery; acknowledging the discomfort while moving forward is often the hardest part of therapy. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure this plan lands well with you. How confident do you feel, on a scale of 1 to 10, that you will actually find five minutes tomorrow morning to do this, and is there anything else you need to feel ready? Also, could you share one quick piece of feedback on how this session felt for you?

I'd say maybe a 7 out of 10? I think I can find the time, but I'm worried I'll talk myself out of it last minute. I don't think I need anything else to feel ready, just have to remind myself why I'm doing this. This session actually felt... kind of eye-opening. I never realized how much my own thoughts were trapping me, so I think that helped a lot.

A seven is a very solid foundation; it balances your awareness of the obstacle with your determination to move forward. Your feedback that this session was eye-opening is incredibly meaningful—it validates that our work together is helping you see the patterns holding you back, which is the first step toward breaking free. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the worry entirely, but to learn how to navigate it so you can act anyway. Thank you for your honesty and courage today; please be gentle with yourself as you prepare for tomorrow, and reach out if that "talking yourself out" voice gets louder than expected. We'll adjust the plan whenever we need to.

Hello, it is great to see you again today. Before we start, I want to briefly check in on how you’ve been feeling since our last session, and then we’ll set a specific goal for today based on what we discussed. Did you get a chance to try writing down your achievements and noting where the doubts came up? If you did, what was your experience like? If not, what do you think would be most useful for us to focus on today?

Hi, thanks for having me. I did try writing down my achievements, but honestly, it felt a bit forced. I listed a few closed deals and good feedback from clients, but then I kept thinking about how John sold three properties last month while I only sold one. It made the list feel pointless.

That honesty about the list feeling forced is incredibly important, and it confirms that simply listing the wins isn't working when the immediate comparison to John dominates your thoughts. It sounds like the moment you saw his recent sales, your brain immediately dismissed your own hard work as irrelevant, which turned your list into a source of friction rather than relief. Given that this specific pattern keeps surfacing, does it feel like we should spend most of today unpacking that automatic comparison to John and testing whether it's actually true, or would you prefer to try a slightly different angle first?

Yeah, I think we should talk about John. It's like no matter how many good things I do, his numbers just sit in my head louder than everything else. I know I shouldn't compare, but it feels automatic, like I can't help it.

It makes total sense that John's numbers feel louder; when a trusted peer succeeds effortlessly, our brains naturally lean toward that narrative because it feels safer than admitting our own path is harder and requires more grit. You mentioned it feels automatic, which is a huge clue—it suggests this isn't a choice you're making consciously, but a reflex your brain uses to protect you from the sting of failure. To figure out if we can change this reflex, let's do a quick experiment: whenever that "John sold three, I sold one" thought pops up, instead of fighting it, could we pause for ten seconds and ask yourself, "Is John actually doing something different, or am I just projecting my own insecurities onto him?" Would you be open to trying that small pause next time the thought arises?

I guess I could try that pause. But I honestly don't know if it'll change anything—it feels like the numbers are just facts, you know? John really did sell three, and I really did sell one. I can pause all I want, but the fact is still there staring me in the face.

You're absolutely right that the numbers are facts; the problem isn't the math, it's how your brain interprets what those numbers *mean* about your worth versus his. When we look at it that way—separating the raw data from the emotional story attached to it—you can see that the comparison feels unfair because it ignores the context of your unique journey. Since we both agree the numbers are real but the *meaning* is where the pain lives, how would you feel if we shifted the focus today from "fixing the comparison" to "understanding what your brain is telling you John represents"? Does that sound like a good starting point?

I think that might help, actually. Because I don't even know why it bothers me so much that it's John specifically. He's not mean or anything—he's actually a decent guy. But every time I see his name on the board, I just feel this tightness in my chest, like I'm falling behind somehow.

That physical tightness you describe is your body reacting to the belief that you are failing, even though the person you're comparing yourself to isn't being hostile. It makes sense that he stands out so vividly; perhaps unconsciously, your brain uses him as a shortcut to judge your entire career rather than looking at the full picture of your hard work. Since we identified that physical sensation as a marker of distress, could we set a specific goal for today to see if focusing on *that* sensation helps us notice the underlying thought causing it? For instance, if we wait until you feel that tightness hit, and then we just name the specific thought ("John is ahead") before analyzing it, would that give us a clear target to work with?

Okay, yes, that sounds like a good plan. I think naming it out loud might actually make it less scary—like if I just say "John is ahead" instead of letting it swirl around in my head, maybe I can see it more clearly. I'm willing to try that.

That is a brilliant intuition; taking a thought out of the abstract fog of your mind and putting it into words creates distance, allowing you to observe it objectively rather than being swept away by its intensity. Since we've agreed that naming the thought and locating the physical sensation are our targets, let's treat today as a live lab where we practice this exact sequence: spot the tension, verbalize the thought, and then challenge it. To ensure we stay on track, would you be comfortable with me suggesting we simulate this scenario right now using a hypothetical situation from your past, or would you prefer to jump straight into a real-time practice later?

Let's try it with a real situation from last week. I remember standing in the break room and seeing the sales board, and that tightness hit me right away. John had three listings up, and I had one. I can feel it again just thinking about it. So right now, I guess the thought is "John is ahead, and I'm not good enough."

Noticing that specific phrase—"John is ahead, and I'm not good enough"—is a major breakthrough because it separates the observation from the judgment, giving us a concrete object to examine rather than a vague feeling. Now that we have named the thought and the physical sensation, let's gently apply the "Fact vs. Meaning" lens we discussed: if we strip away the emotional story, what is the literal truth of the situation versus what your brain assumes it means about your competence? Specifically, does the fact that John has three listings mean anything about your ability to close deals, or does it only reflect his current inventory or timing? Which part feels more reliable to you?

Well, when you put it like that... it's just a fact that he has more listings right now. It doesn't mean I'm bad at my job. I've closed deals before, and I'll close more. I guess I just assume his numbers mean he's better, but maybe it's just a timing thing. That feels a little bit like relief, honestly.

That relief is a powerful signal that you are successfully separating the raw data (his listings) from the emotional story (you are inadequate); your brain was trying to predict a disaster, but the new perspective offers a safer, more realistic alternative. Since we've clarified that the tightness comes from the *interpretation*, not the numbers themselves, let's solidify a concrete tool to use next time: instead of letting the comparison run wild, could we agree to verbally state, "His numbers reflect his timing, not my worth," the moment the chest tightens? Would you like to practice saying that line out loud right now to build the muscle memory?

Sure, I can try that. "His numbers reflect his timing, not my worth." It feels a little awkward saying it out loud, but I guess that's because it's new. Maybe if I say it enough times, it'll start to feel more natural.

That is exactly the kind of growth we see in therapy; what feels awkward today becomes a familiar ally tomorrow because your brain learns to trust the new phrase. Since repetition is key, let's lock this into a specific trigger for tonight: whenever you glance at the sales board and feel that familiar tightness, take a deep breath and silently whisper that exact phrase to yourself three times. Does committing to that specific ritual tonight feel doable for you?
Yeah, I think I can do that. Three times sounds simple enough. I'll try it tonight when I check the board before leaving. Thanks for walking me through this—it actually feels a bit lighter now.

It is wonderful to hear that the session feels lighter; that sense of relief often comes from realizing that the tightness wasn't a reflection of your actual performance, but rather the result of a specific, manageable thought pattern. Before we conclude, I want to ensure we are fully aligned on the plan: tonight, when you see the board, you will catch the tightness, whisper "His numbers reflect his timing, not my worth" three times, and then step away from the board to prevent the spiral from continuing. Does that sound like a clear and achievable goal for tonight?
Yes, that sounds clear. I'll do exactly that. And I appreciate you not just telling me to stop comparing, but actually helping me understand why I do it. That makes a big difference.

You are very welcome, and I completely agree that explaining the "why" behind the habit is far more effective than just commanding you to stop it; understanding that your brain is using a faulty shortcut makes the new habit feel like a logical upgrade rather than a moral failing. Since we have a clear plan for tonight and you feel lighter, is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up, or are you ready to head out with this new perspective?
